speechtext: Orx the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister and ask him whether he would give the house and the country a statement as to the present position of negotiations as between the C.P.R. and the union officials and also an indication as to the nature of the plan which he submitted to them and which is now the subject of consideration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is preferable to say little at this time about the negotiations. They have been informal negotiations which I have found, not to my surprise at all but to my satisfaction, were perhaps more conducive to bringing about a feeling between the parties that an earnest effort should be made by them to overcome the narrow margin between their respective attitudes. The plan would be one to have the operations resumed at the earliest possible moment and to have them resumed on the terms of a contract that would be practically along the lines of the contract entered into between the same union and the Canadian National Railways last June for the period up to March 31, 1958, with a provision that the same diesel rule would be in that contract but would be subject to renegotiation in the light of the report of a board that would be set up by the government to investigate the aspects of the diesel rule that are not agreed

to by both parties. The details that I trust both parties will find it in the interests of Canada generally to agree to are being discussed and worked out, and there would not be a reference until there has been the greatest possible measure of agreement by the parties as to what the terms of reference should be.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: If I might ask a supplementary question, when was the suggestion by the Prime Minister in order to bring these two groups together in agreement submitted? Was it suggested at the time the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour met with representatives of the C.P.R. and the union or was it submitted for the first time yesterday or the day before? Would the Prime Minister also say what he means, and what he meant yesterday, when he stated there was only a slight margin of difference between the parties? What is the margin of difference to which he referred?

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
It is the
same suggestion that was made at the first meeting of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as acting prime minister, and the Minister of Labour with the parties on the last Saturday of the year. It has been discussed and certain aspects of it have been the subject of suggestions by both parties that would imply some variation in the details. I feel convinced that the only point at issue now is whether there should be a contractual undertaking by both parties to accept and write into their modified agreement something that would be in conformity with the findings of the investigating board appointed by the government.
I am not sure whether or not I said it yesterday, but the objection of the union is that it is tantamount to their acceptance of compulsory arbitration. The objection of the railway company to that not being a contractual undertaking now is that if they do riot make it a contractual undertaking the dispute could start all over again. I have been urging that is not a realistic view to take. If there is a thorough investigation and report, neither side is going to attempt, after that, to hold out on a formula for safe operations that will have been recommended after a full investigation by a board that would be constituted in such a way as to have considerable prestige with Canadian public opinion.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: I have one more question. As to the nature of the board, is that to be the board of transport commissioners or an independent board to be set up composed of representatives of the government, the railway and the union?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
The possibilities with respect to the two kinds of board the hon. gentleman mentioned have been under consideration. There is such a volume of work before the board of transport commissioners that that has been one reason for not asking them to set everything else aside and devote quite a long period to this problem, because it will take some time to make a full investigation that will be such as to satisfy the public that it has been given every possible consideration before a recommendation is made.
There is more than one statute under which that kind of board could be set up. Under the Railway Act it could be a reference to the board of transport commissioners. Under the industrial disputes act it could be a board constituted by the Minister of Labour, under one of the sections of that act. There is also, of course, the general Inquiries Act, under which a royal commission could be set up. What is being pressed, I will say, by us is something that will be apt to be accepted without compulsion having to be resorted to.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: And is the decision final?

speechtext: There will not be any agreement accepted by the union of a contractual obligation to accept the decision, but Canadian citizens usually accept what properly constituted authority determines to be the right kind of law for the land.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill). Was permission to enter Canada recently refused to one C. G. Hanna at a west coast port? If so, on what grounds?
Would the minister also advise as to the present whereabouts and status of that unfortunate individual?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: C. G. HANNA  REASON FOR REFUSAL TO ADMIT
speechtext:
I wonder if I might have Your Honour's permission to answer this question notwithstanding a ruling you


made at a previous session that you would not permit questions about individual immigration cases.
There has been a most extraordinary amount of publicity about the case of this unfortunate young man and I think perhaps hon. members would like to be in possession of the real facts.
He has on three different occasions appeared on a merchant ship at a Canadian port. He is in no way admissible to Canada under the Immigration Act and in fact at least four or five different provisions of the act would have to be set aside if he were to be admitted to this country. In view of the fact that he had no connection with anyone in this country, that he was on the ship of a highly civilized country and there were no doubt other places in the world where it would be possible for him to go, it did not seem to me it would be a proper thing for me to disregard the law enacted by this parliament and to seek by some back-door method to get around the law which was made by this parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) who has most ably moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
(Translation):
Also, Mr. Speaker, my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) for having carried out his task equally well when seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

The Address-Mr. Cauchon
At the time of the great fire in the town of Salaberry of Valleyfield, on December 30, last, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) sent a message of sympathy to the families who had lost their homes. On their behalf and also speaking for myself, I want to express our sincere appreciation to him. It is comforting to realize the spirit of good-will that is shown in such circumstances, for without the heroic efforts of our firemen and of those who volunteered to help in one way or another, our town would certainly have had to deplore a much larger misfortune.
(Text):
As in speeches of former sessions, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne has expressed the Liberal government's policy of promoting social welfare and economic development and of effecting the continuance of the prosperity our country has enjoyed under the wise guidance of its capable Liberal leaders. An outstanding example of this guidance applied internationally was the plan submitted to the United Nations by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) at a time when that body was, I would say, nearly paralysed by war in the Middle East and Hungary. As one Canadian newspaperman said, "This week Canadians at the United Nations in New York have good reason to be proud to be Canadians." Never, Mr. Speaker, was constructive leadership more needed than at that moment and the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his Canadian delegation gave that leadership.
Although the opposition may refuse to our administrators the credit so justly theirs, it cannot deny that Canada has had prosperity; nor can it deny that foresight, good administration and sound financing have resulted in unprecedented progress within the last two decades. What is more, steps have been taken to assure Canada's continued prosperity. Think, Mr. Speaker, of the two great projects now under way, one to give the west eastern markets for its great resources of natural gas, the other to develop the great hydro power resources of the east and at the same time to give the lakehead direct access to the Atlantic seaboard.
These gigantic undertakings, together with the ever increasing amity among Canadians of different national origins, have served to convince all Canadians that the Prime Minister (Mr. St'. Laurent) has done more to unite, both tangibly and intangibly, the people and the geographical units of this vast country than has any other Canadian. In the annals of of Canada I am sure he will be accorded that honour for all time.

In justice too, I must pay a well merited tribute to our Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) who has so skilfully led the house in its deliberations and the country through a time of dangerous inflationary trends. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and other ministers have also, with courage and fortitude in the face of determined opposition, taken measures to assure Canada's economic development.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, one immediately thinks of the Hon. Lionel Chevrier and the seaway authority. In April, 1951, I spoke to him of my constituency's interest in the work to be undertaken and voiced our objections to lift bridges at St. Louis de Gonzague, on Larocque road and at Meloche-ville where increasingly heavy traffic would be dangerously impeded. At that time he promised to study the matter and, Mr. Speaker, as a result I was pleased to be able to announce last year that we could be assured of a tunnel at Melocheville. I hope also to be able to announce that something will be done at the other two points. On behalf of my riding of Beauharnois-Salaberry I wish to thank the Hon. Mr. Chevrier and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler).
That part of Quebec which I have the honour to represent now has, as I have formerly intimated, unrivalled industrial sites. The tremendous combined navigation-power project now under construction together with power now available, a skilled reliable labour force, a productive countryside, almost unlimited water supplies and an excellent situation in respect to markets should be most attractive both to light and heavy industries seeking new sites or working out plans for decentralization.
My foregoing remarks were preliminary to the introduction of a subject that has been of sincere concern to me for some years, that is, the practice of discrimination against the older but employable worker. Though I have no intention of reiterating the facts I presented in 1951, I feel it my duty to say that this discrimination continues and seeks justification for the same reasons as then. Proof of my assertion may be found in the advertisements of our daily newspapers.
We must concede that evolution of a population through the complex stages of its economic development and the continuing industrial revolution with the resultant increase in automation give rise to many difficult problems, but problems nonetheless necessary of resolution.
Then too we must accept the idea that a nation's progress depends upon (1) higher production with a corresponding rise in living standards for all and (2) new outlets for the

investment capital which provides new jobs and skills not only for the young but for those still employable who have been thrown out of work by changed production methods or similar causes.
All workers should and must share equally in job opportunities created by our present economic growth. Canada's citizens, even those 41 to 60, should have equal opportunities in its labour markets; that is, of course, if age is not a bona fide occupational limitation. Both government and private enterprise, therefore, have the task of anticipating and resolving problems arising from this continuing evolution, especially problems pertaining to the unemployment of any section of Canadian labour.
Because I have kept myself well informed regarding the employment situation in my own industrial community, it is clear to me that workers over 40 are most frequently the sufferers when production methods change. Consequently I have followed closely the attempts of various governments to check discrimination because of age. Recently I have read "New Channels for the Golden Years", a document issued by the New York state joint legislative committee on problems of the aging, under the chairmanship of Senator Thomas Desmond. Among the recommendations made on page 7 of the report there are two of particular interest. They are:
That the state encourage industry to establish vested pension plans and move in that direction itself in connection with the state retirement system.
That the state recognize the greater difficulty older persons have in finding jobs by providing an unemployment insurance differential for those over 40.
On page 10 the advantages of a vested pension plan are thus described:
Our committee believes that vested pension plans hold forth promise of
(a)	increasing likelihood of employers hiring workers at ages 55, 60 and over;
(b)	preventing indigency in later life resulting from workers changing employment in firms which grant pensions only after lengthy service;
(c)	reducing pressure on government to take drastic action such as adopting an old age pension act.
The British national advisory committee on employment of older men and women after studying the problem also has emphasized the need of "preserving pension rights on change of employment." The committee later in the report makes a recommendation that the state expand its anti-discrimination law to include age, as does that of the state of Massachusetts. Moreover, the following recommendation is also made as found on page 23 of the same report:
To give further emphasis to our belief that the state should move to end discriminatory practices
The Address-Mr. Cauchon
in employment of the 40-plus, we recommend:
That the state should bar any company from bidding on state construction, equipment, service or other contracts if it discriminates against the 40-plus;
The burden and stigma placed on our free enterprise system by the crude, raw, unscientific policy of banning the employment of the 40-plus by modern industry, particularly big industries, and especially new industries, warrants society, through its elective officials, in taking steps effectively to prevent such personnel policies.
To the contention, "But it costs industry more money to hire the 40-plus", we reply, "These are costs industry and society must bear".
If the cost of employment of the 40-plus is increased prices, we need to add that to our costs, just as we have added to the cost of production the cost of sanitary, safe factories, social security taxes, shorter work week.
However, we have seen no evidence that hiring the 40-plus will increase the cost of production. We have seen figures indicating that workmen's compensation costs rise, but these have been disproved.
We have seen figures that group insurance costs rise, but these do not appear significant.
We have seen figures that pension costs rise when the 40-plus are hired, but we have not seen them balanced against any compensating figures reflecting lower absenteeism, the greater loyalty, the greater stability, the lower turnover rate, the increased know-how of the older worker.
Nor have we seen what the cost to industry would be if vested pensions were adopted so that the employer hiring a man at 55 would not have to feel he had to provide "a suitable pension" for him at 65, but only a 10-year pension.
I was also interested to see by the 1955 report of the International Labour Organization that the state of Massachusetts had almost eliminated all discrimination in employment practices, including that against age.
In order to learn more about the Massachusetts law I went to Boston last spring to gather at first hand information from the officers of the commission.
It might be well at this point to summarize briefly the Massachusetts Fair Employment Practice Act and its amendment, sponsored by the American Federation of Labour, to include age. Age is defined as being between 45 and 65.
Every employer, employment agency and labour union subject to the provisions of the law must post it conspicuously on its premises. Those not subject are employers with fewer than six persons, clubs, et cetera not organized for private profit, domestic servants, and those employed in family businesses. The law reads as follows:
No person shall be denied the right to work because of race, colour, religious creed, national origin, age or ancestry.
In respect to age, it is illegal for employers or employment agencies to: (1) ask questions before employment which directly or indirectly disclose age; (2) to print or circulate advertisements which directly or indirectly

The Address-Mr. Cauchon specify limitation because of age, unless that limitation is based upon a bona fide occupational qualification; (3) in case of employers to discharge or refuse to hire an individual because of age; (4) to act unfairly against an individual in matters relating to compensation, terms of employment et cetera because of age.
Labour organizations and groups of employees are forbidden to exclude from membership or to resist employment of such persons.
Moreover-and this is important-the law hag been interpreted to apply even if a company had, prior to its passing, adopted a retirement or pension plan calling for the retirement of persons between those ages, 45-65.
The commission seeks to gain compliance with the law by means of conference, conciliation and persuasion. A commissioner is assigned to investigate each complaint. Only once has a public hearing of a case been necessary. Public acceptance of the law has been due principally to the educational program initiated by the commission which arranges conferences with groups affected in various communities. In addition, surveys of the industrial communities are made by small committees of their own citizens, serving without remuneration. These acquaint the commission with problems peculiar to each locality. The surveys also tend to arouse interest and to enlist the co-operation of those affected by the law.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I might say that Pennsylvania has also enacted a similar statute.
As a result of my study of this question, I would make the following recommendations:
1.	That the Department of Labour should begin a study of the Massachusetts commission against discrimination with a view to setting up a similar commission in Canada.
2.	That the department should also consider amending the national Unemployment Insurance Act to enable the worker to change employment without loss of his rights in a pension plan.
Possibly pension stamps could be affixed to the workers' unemployment insurance books together with the unemployment insurance stamps. Whatever system is adopted, it should effectively protect the senior members of our society from discrimination and assure them of pension upon their retirement.
We cannot permit industry to make a unilateral decision to oust or to exclude middle-aged workers from jobs. Jobs can, in some cases, be adapted to the workers; in others, the workers can be trained for new jobs.
It is the inherent duty of each Canadian to discharge the responsibilities of citizenship.


It is equally the right of each Canadian to contribute to and share in his country's progress and prosperity. I believe it is industry's and government's joint responsibility, in recognition of the innate dignity of the human soul, to provide employment for each worker during the years he is employable and to assure him of a pension sufficient to free him from want in his old age.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the first speaker of the Conservative party to follow our new leader I wish formally for the record of this house to congratulate him on his new position and naturally, without any reservation, to wish him all the success in the world. The last two days here and outside the house have certainly shown that his fine qualities and capabilities will now be made known to all in this country. I want to say also that we extend to our retired leader the best wishes for complete restoration in the future of that good health that he knew formerly. I wish to congratulate too, Mr. Speaker, the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robi-chaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. There were remarks made by both these hon. members which I thought were very fair. They called attention to some of the problems I have in my own -constituency.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), in speaking of the city of Edmonton, said that they were indeed fortunate to have such fine prosperity and growth in that area. It was my pleasure to be in Edmonton a few weeks ago and I can say that is true. I commend him for further suggesting in this regard that perhaps their problems were not as great as those of some other areas.
The seconder, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), who is from my home province of New Brunswick, suggested that there is a new optimism in our province which has replaced the old pessimism. I agree with him. I commend him also for having received that new spirit.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not point out some of the difficulties that still exist in the Saint John area, in the province of New Brunswick and also in the maritime provinces. I do not wish to be thought pessimistic, but these are problems that have of late taken serious and grave form. At the outset, I want to say that these problems which I will mention are economic and geographic in nature; that is agreed. However, I would suggest, in the second place, that there is a grave federal responsibility in each of these serious problems-perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it

could be better described as a lack of federal responsibility for these ills that are creeping into our economic life in an area that is not quite as fortunate as the area mentioned by the mover of the address yesterday.
Our sad story begins about one year ago when we had a serious strike at the Atlantic sugar refinery in Saint John. There were 700 men out of work and 16 working days were lost. It was a wage dispute and was settled at Christmas of 1955. I am not taking sides in the matter. I only want to point out what was stated by management at that time, and I do not think it has been seriously disputed by anybody connected with that matter. It was stated that two problems exist for an industry in such an area as the maritimes. They were out of the immediate marketing area for their product and the difficulties with respect to their competitors were greatly increased. Secondly, there was the problem which a new survey had shown would be felt when the St. Lawrence seaway was opened.
Next, we had a strike during the same period on the Princess Helene, the C.P.R. vessel which connects Saint John and western Nova Scotia at Digby. There were 80 days lost. The strike ended in December 1955 and it was later settled in the spring of last year when wage talks resumed after the vessel returned to service. Again the problem there was one of economics and geography. The strike, to a large degree, was managed by a gentleman who is well known to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and others in this house by the name of Hal Banks. Direction for that strike,-again I am not taking sides, but I am simply trying to point out the position in which we were and how it was misunderstood-came from Montreal by telephone and the strikers did not even know when they should begin the strike. This was the first waterfront strike we had had since the seamen's union of 1949, but it was felt by all in the community of New Brunswick and also in Nova Scotia.
The third serious situation, Mr. Speaker, came to a head on November 14 of this past year when a public meeting was held in Saint John with respect to the very serious lay-offs at the Saint John dry dock, our important shipbuilding industry. I think perhaps I could best explain this by reading a resolution that was passed at that time and agreed upon by all concerned who were attending that meeting.
Whereas the Saint John dry dock is one of the most important sources of employment and purchasing power in the Saint John area:
And whereas employment at the dry dock is at a very low level with only some 300 employees as against more than 900 a year ago and a full employment level of more than 1,300:
The Address-Mr. Bell
And whereas the present situation represents a weekly payroll decline of more than $40,000 in comparison with last year;
And whereas this condition severely affects many other industries and commercial establishments in Saint John;
Therefore be it resolved:
That an appeal be directed to the proper authorities, civic, provincial, and federal, that special arrangements be made forthwith to place with the dry dock contracts which will ensure a higher level of employment and so relieve a most difficult situation for the employees and which will also aid in improving the purchasing power of the community of greater Saint John.
I do not wish to go into the details of that situation which has already been brought to the attention of the house, but I simply want to say that at that meeting it was brought out, and agreed by all concerned, that one of the main difficulties was a $3.50 freight differential with the various other competitors of this shipbuilding industry in Canada. We also know that the related problem of a Canadian merchant navy is connected with it. However, I do want to mention one aspect of this meeting which calls attention, I hope, to the problem I am pressing here today of the lack of federal responsibility. I refer to a telegram that was sent by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) to that gathering when he had been asked to attend or send a nominee. This is a telegram from the Hon. George C. Marler, addressed to the secretary-treasurer of local No. 3, Industrial Union of Marine and Shipbuilding Workers:
Regret that I am unable personally to attend meeting Saint John Wednesday, November 14 and do not think any useful purpose would be served by sending representative of my department. The Canadian maritime commission is fully aware of the situation at Saint John dry dock and is making every effort to see whether it is possible to find some work which could be allocated to it.
George Marler
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, the workers who were finding it hard to make ends meet were not too pleased with this telegram. However, I do not wish to be hard on the Minister of Transport at the present time because he has shown interest in Saint John, and he has made two or three trips there since taking his position.
I now come to the most important and gravest aspect of our problem, namely, the present C.P.R. strike. I think the difficulties of the community of Saint John are well known to the nation at the present time. The strike was a double blow to our community because we also have shipping as well as railway facilities to consider. In addition, thousands of refugees were coming to our shores and they further congested the efforts that we were making to use the small Canadian National Railway facilities there. Seven daily freight trains had to be laid off. The C.P.R. employees, who number

The Address-Mr. Bell nearly 2,000, are all out of work as a result of the strike, and over 2,000 longshoremen are being thrown out of work at the present time because of ship diversions at the height of our very busy winter port season. Extra staff has been taken on at our unemployment insurance office. It is a serious blow that we have received, and it recalls to our minds the situation 35 or 40 years ago when we also had similar difficulties. Perhaps an indication of the seriousness of it, if any further word needs to be given, is the fact that prayers have been said in churches to help relieve the hardship which has resulted.
This is a permanent money loss to our city. It is not just the case of the $50,000 a day that we shall be losing. It is a fact that we can never recover this business and this money which we so sorely need. The longshoremen in our area live on credit from one season to the next. They have a busy peak season, and when ships are lost to other ports and when we know that the backlog cannot be caught up until the St. Lawrence opens we realize it is a permanent blow. In this connection, I have telegrams from the mayors of the city of Saint John and the city of Lancaster which explain the declaration that was made by both of their common councils with respect to the C.P.R. strike, and which state formally that an emergency condition existed in both of those cities. I will not put these on the record, Mr. Speaker, but I also just received a telegram explaining the seriousness of the strike in western Nova Scotia. This telegram was received from the affiliated boards of trade in the Annapolis valley, which was a joint effort, and probably speaks for the whole of the western Nova Scotia communities. This is the story of this serious strike. I have dealt with it from the local aspect. Then we can go on to the provincial aspect of it. I could probably refer to any area of the province, but surely we would be entitled to go to the constituency of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) who knows what some of these difficulties are with regard to layoffs and some of the other problems which I have mentioned.
We remember the serious layoffs that resulted two or three years ago from the shutdown of the cotton mill in Marysville; we remember some of the efforts that were made, but we also remember the lack of consideration that the federal government gave to this serious problem of ours. The Minister of Labour probably is not happy today when he knows that in the town of McAdam in his constituency over 92 per cent of the 3,000

inhabitants are completely dependent on the C.P.R. payroll. He cannot be happy about that. I am not taking the time now to refer to other problems; I am simply saying that this strike is affecting the entire province of New Brunswick.
Then we come to the maritime aspect of this problem. I have mentioned some of the local difficulties we have had; I have mentioned some of the provincial difficulties, and I now wish to refer to one of the serious problems that we have faced in the mari-times because of the hard money policy of the Bank of Canada and of this government. The best way that it can be explained, probably, is to refer to a statement that one of our people made at the time when he said that there is a family of 10 children and one of the children of that family happens to be taken ill. The present government gives the whole 10 children a dose of castor oil. We are of the opinion in the maritimes that we have never known inflation, and various statistics which have been given here and which will be given later will prove that. We object very strongly to this hard money policy which cripples us much more than it cripples some of the other expanding areas of this country. Our premier has objected strongly to this policy. He has made approaches to the Prime Minister and little attention has been given to it by this government. We do have that on the record.
I also wish to refer to the present upward revision of freight rates. For the first time in the history of the Atlantic provinces the four premiers, two Conservative now and two Liberal, got together and gave a joint statement of objection to the new increase in freight rates. This is a serious problem. It is one that we feel very strongly. The old benefits of the Maritime Freight Rates Act are no longer helpful to us, and those horizontal increases are making it extremely difficult for us to compete in the central Canadian markets. It is another example of the economic difficulty we have, and which is recognized but which also bears a lack of federal interest.
I refer to another recent announcement, Mr. Speaker, which was made when the statistics of the Department of National Revenue were given at the end of 1956 dealing with the incomes of 56 Canadian cities. We noted that Halifax was in 46th position, Moncton 47th and Saint John 51st. This is another indication of the economic difficulties of the maritime provinces.
Then we also remember the story of the election in Nova Scotia and I imagine this matter will be given better treatment by

The Address

Mr. Bell
those who know more about it. However, we remember the story of the former premier's last desperate despondent attempt to avoid the inevitable defeat which he saw coming. He came here to Ottawa to see the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) ostensibly on behalf of all the maritime premiers but he really came here to see if something could be done not only in order to save the Liberal party in Nova Scotia but to try and do something for the entire region. At that time the Prime Minister was quoted as saying to the then premier of Nova Scotia:
The making of direct expenditures toward the improvement of the economy of a particular area by the federal government would be justifiable if it were felt that the indirect results of such expenditure would develop the economy of Canada as a whole.
The Prime Minister was reported as saying this in the Daily Gleaner on September 6 1956.
Well, Mr. Speaker, needless to say nothing was done about that and the Liberal government went down to bitter defeat in Nova Scotia. In that same connection we remember a statement the Prime Minister made at the labour convention which I think was held in April of last year, a statement that has often been referred to in this house, to the effect that initiative should come from the people in the maritimes. We took that statement at its face value in an honest way because most maritimers are honest and we then proceeded to make our proposals and many were made.
One proposal which we have been making in New Brunswick for many years concerns power development. The Beechwood project has been brought here in a non-partisan way together with the complete facts, our proposals and our formulas, and nothing has been done about it.
I can think of several ways in which the Prime Minister could have taken action if the statements he made at the labour convention and to the former premier of Nova Scotia were true. I can think of a complete new revision of our freight rates; I can think of a further interest on the part of the federal government in fostering traffic through our maritime ports. Protected and subsidized industries in Canada still continue to use United States ports for a great deal of their export and import business. These are but a few of the ways in which the Prime Minister could bring about the intention of his words.
At the same time, however, we should be fair enough to recognize that in the throne speech this year there is mention of a proposed plan to assist in the solution of our agricultural problems. If it is successful the committee of the Senate will deal with and 82715-5J
consider the better use of land for agriculture to contribute more effectively to the improvement of agricultural production and the income of those engaged in it.
The Prime Minister referred to the problems of the farmers in Quebec and these are similar to the problems facing the farmers in New Brunswick and other parts of the maritimes. The government is finally making an effort to do something concerning these problems which have been brought to the attention of this house time and time again. Of course it is late and it comes just before the election but I suppose we must put in some kind words here concerning the fact that the government is considering this matter.
The Prime Minister mentioned, and rightly so, some of the problems which exist in Quebec. We have many French speaking Canadians in the province of New Brunswick; they constitute nearly 50 per cent of our population. I suppose they will benefit from the farming improvements that might be made and they will also benefit from any interest the Prime Minister and others take in their particular problems. I might point out, however, that we have other specific problems in this country many of which exist in the maritimes. I am merely saying that we should have from this government action that will bear out the intention of the words that have been spoken by the Prime Minister and others on many occasions.
I have mentioned the local problems in Saint John, I have mentioned the provincial problems that exist in the maritimes, and I have mentioned problems from a strictly maritime standpoint. I recognize that peculiar economic and geographic difficulties exist but I suggest there has been a lack of federal responsibility in these matters.
Probably the most important problem confronting us and requiring immediate attention is the strike. I have tried to deal fairly with it from a strictly local aspect. In the light of what has been said inside and outside of this house, in the light of the meeting that was held yesterday between the president of the C.P.R. and the Prime Minister, in the light of the meetings that have been held with the union and in the light of the indications the Prime Minister mentioned both yesterday and today that a solution will soon be forthcoming, I now ask the Prime Minister to come out and let us have the solution. It is there; they know what the plan is and what the answer must be. Let us have it. My people in Saint John want the strike settled. It has been suggested there is a solution that will soon be forthcoming. Is it coming this afternoon, tomorrow or the next day? Is the government waiting around with it so that they

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) on their splendid speeches in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.


In the next few minutes I hope to place before hon. members mostly items of interest in my own riding, leaving world affairs to others so much better versed in such matters.
I would like at this time to say to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) that although competition between the ports of Saint John and Halifax is always very keen it is always friendly and while we in Halifax are benefitting at the present time and Saint John is losing we wish to say to the hon. member we get no glory out of such increases in business and we join with him in hoping the strike may be ended very soon.
On Tuesday my colleague and I attended the unveiling ceremony of the monument to honour the memory of a great Canadian, the late Sir Robert Borden, a former distinguished prime minister of Canada, who served his country through the critical and anxious years of the first world war and represented Halifax honourably and ably from 1896 to 1904 and again from 1908 to 1917. It is only meet and right that we should honour our great men, for a wise nation preserves its records and remembers the sacrifices and glories of the past.
As the year 1957 opens, we have in Canada a situation of extraordinary buoyancy. Few Canadians are suffering because of broad economic or business problems. There are situations, as there always will be, where an individual or an industry is affected unfavourably, but on the whole Canadians find themselves in a fortunate economic position. The province of Nova Scotia and the other Atlantic provinces have participated in this general growth and expansion and a spirit of optimism prevails generally and we are very much gratified over this situation.
What is far more important at the moment and of greater significance for the future is the practical and tangible recognition by the government of Canada of the disparity in economic circumstances as between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada. This recognition has taken the form of imaginative measures which in some cases represent extensions of established policies and in others represent an altogether new approach.
We were all pleased with the announcement made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) concerning the government's intention to spend an extra $270,000 in its 1957 tourist promotion budget for the specific purpose of encouraging more vacational travel in the Atlantic provinces. This in addition to the Bluenose service between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor, this ship having been constructed

through the co-operation of the government of the province, will give a boost to the tourist trade in Nova Scotia.
Another forward step is the acquisition of the Grand Pre park which I believe is to be operated as a federal park.
A further step in the development of our fisheries is indicated by the recent announcement of an extension of the subsidy to provide for loans for the larger vessels. To parallel this assistance to the larger operators I think the development program for the inshore fishermen should be stepped up. To put this suggestion in concrete form and based on the experience in my own constituency, I think the need for federally assisted bait freezers and cold storage facilities for Halifax east and west should be examined. If there is a need for additional facilities which would assist iri the sound economic development of our fisheries resources, let us make every reasonable effort to encourage sound growth.
On December 30 a terrific wind storm struck Nova Scotia wrecking great numbers of fishing boats and lobster traps. I have had many letters from fishermen who have suffered to an extent far beyond their means of recuperation. They have asked for assistance in becoming rehabilitated. I appreciate that this is probably riot within the scope of the federal authority but I would ask that our fisheries inspectors and officers do everything they possibly can to assist and that the federal government draw to the attention of the proper provincial authorities the necessity of a close survey and the urgent need of financial assistance.
On previous occasions in this house I have expressed regret at the relative lack of impact on the Atlantic provinces of the industrial development bank. This was evident from the small proportion of total loans going to firms in those provinces. I was delighted at the decision to open a branch of the bank to serve the Atlantic region. I know from the bank's operations, even since June of last year, that its facilities are being more widely used. The reports indicate a very satisfactory public reaction to the administration of the affairs of the bank in Halifax. Perhaps as experience within the present policy develops there may emerge a broad program of development going beyond the existing program which would involve detailed planning on a broad basis.
While on the subject I should like to make a comment on the volume of foreign investment in Canada, particularly United States capital. I know of no community or township which would not welcome a new factory or new resources development,
The Address

Mr. Balcom whether financed by Canadian, United States, or funds of other nationalities. Efforts are being made now by provincial and local officials to interest United States or other financial groups in our forest resources. We have an excellent working force, one that is second to none, and there is ample power, either at hand or available on short notice.
Another recent statement of interest to maritimers was the Prime Minister's (Mr. St. Laurent's) reference to an inquiry into the problem of land use and development in eastern Canada. I hope that a comprehensive inquiry will include an examination of soil conservation and flood control to include fresh water areas. There is one area in Halifax county, the Musquodoboits, which has a well established farming and lumbering economy which could benefit greatly from a properly conceived plan and managed flood control. Opportunities for development would then be much greater and more numerous if there were proper conservation and flood control.
While on this subject I should like to emphasize that these forward moves are not falling on barren ground. The Atlantic provinces jointly and severally are eager to do their parts as individuals, as companies, as associations, as communities or as provinces in order to develop their opportunities. Thirty years ago the maritime board of trade and the three provincial governments joined forces to set up the maritimes transportation commission. The purpose was to have an agency whose sole job was to give service to maritimers on freight rate problems. The commission now also includes Newfoundland.
Two years ago, again at the instigation of the maritime provinces board of trade, the four provincial premiers presided, so to speak, at the birth of the Atlantic provinces economic council or, in short, APEC, an organization of businessmen dedicated to improving economic conditions in the Atlantic provinces. The spirit of co-operation has grown since then and with it enthusiasm for the promotional objects of this economic council.
With government, labour, agriculture and industry all working together, I feel that the four Atlantic provinces are on the march. We do not wish for any special treatment from Ottawa but we do want the opportunity to carry on and to have the Atlantic region live and prosper with the other parts of this great dominion.
In the consideration of broad national policies which takes place in the debate on the speech from the throne, we always find ourselves providing for one phase or another of our transportation problem. This is

The Address-Mr. Balcom not surprising when you realize that transportation was one of the cornerstones of confederation and over the years has been a major preoccupation of government. It comes in many guises-railways, airlines, canals, ferries, port facilities and so on.
Today I want to speak about some matters in this field which though of a local and regional nature are nonetheless an important part of the national program. The first is the Maritime Freight Hates Act. Since 1927, when the act was passed, many changes have taken place. The benefits that were intended under the act have been reduced or whittled away by the effects of the so-called horizontal freight rate increases that have taken place since the war. Developments in other parts of Canada have contributed to this trend. Since the railways are not able to raise rates where intense truck and water competition exists, they must obtain their additional revenue where competition is less keen. So the pyramid grows. With the addition of the St. Lawrence seaway to the facilities of the central provinces their relative position will improve faster in comparison with other parts of Canada.
It is time then for another look and not only a look, Mr. Speaker, but a searching examination of the actual effects of the act as it now stands. Let me remind the house that this piece of legislation was not a special sop to an area because we happened to be less well off than other parts of Canada. The reduction in rates was based on a judgment of the amount of compensation required to make up for the circuitous route of the rail line, a route chosen for strategic purposes and reasons as opposed to the requirements of commerce.
This matter has been discussed in the house before by myself and other members from the east. It was brought to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) early last summer by the Hon. Mr. Hicks of Nova Scotia, speaking on behalf of the four Atlantic provinces. The royal commission on Canada's economic prospects has been asked to consider the problem and we await with interest their findings on this matter. I would emphasize that this is not a question to be argued before the board of transport commissioners. It is rather a matter of the highest government policy to be dealt with on the basis of thorough and expert examination of the whole transportation problem in the Atlantic provinces.
I would here commend also the improvement and increase in grain handling facilities at the port of Halifax. Substantial additions are also under way to the facilities on the Dartmouth side of the harbour. It is

time now, in the over-all planning for port development, that more attention be paid to related projects which involve the town of Dartmouth and the municipality of the county of Halifax. Along the waterfront from Dartmouth to Eastern Passage there are major industrial and defence establishments. Imperial Oil Limited has just opened a modern refinery, double the capacity of the previous one, with an added investment of over $30 million. Irving Oil has added storage and wharf facilities. We have Fairey Aviation Limited, a progressive and well-managed aircraft organization, and the Shearwater naval base is also situated there. All the attendant traffic has been added to the demands of normal growth. This has created problems which cannot fairly be regarded as the sole responsibility of the local authorities. In the interests of assuring the best use of harbour facilities as well as making proper provision for defence, federal assistance in planning and financing additional road facilities is, I consider, warranted.
Further, in connection with the strategic position of Halifax, the necessity for road transport facilities in time of emergency should be considered. There is not much point in having expensive vehicles for transport if they can be quickly immobilized for lack of roads. I know that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) is anxious to see the trans-Canada highway a national asset. I suggest that defence considerations call for the extension of that highway from Truro to Halifax. I am led to believe by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Purdy) that Truro is gaining so much in importance that it will eventually be the capital of Nova Scotia. This road from Truro to Halifax would be in addition to the road to Sydney.
In a growing country like Canada we can never stand still. We must always improve and go forward. There is immediate need for improvement of the Canadian National Railways facilities at the centre of maritime activity, Halifax. If the baggage and express operations are not the heart of the service, they are certainly the most obvious to the public. The freight office and yards in the north end of the city may affect more lives, but I am sure more of the public see and go through the old wooden structures which are an eyesore in a modern community and certainly cannot be a credit to an important organization like the C.N.R. Nor do they speak well for the efficiency of that great enterprise.
I might also make a suggestion at this point concerning the Nova Scotian hotel. It is a well known fact the Halifax hotels have a

high occupancy rate and that accommodation is pitifully lacking. Undoubtedly this has a deterrent effect on general business and in particular the tourist business on which both federal and provincial governments are spending substantial sums to develop it. It seems to me that a relatively minor expenditure in terms of over-all investment by the C.N.R. could add much-needed rooms and conference facilities as well. With the overhead expenses carried by more patrons, it is most likely that such an addition would improve the operating cost picture as well. The need for facilities is well known. Why not move ahead now?
Before leaving this subject I want to refer briefly to the use made of Canadian ports by our manufacturers. Of course, coming from the east, naturally I am interested in the ports of Saint John and Halifax. I think this is important because it is a situation that can be controlled. By that I mean that with the transportation facilities which belong to the nation and which have been built largely at public expense and are available at comparable prices, it is to the advantage of all that shippers direct their cargoes via Canadian ports.
I should like to cite a few examples where the Canadian public has a right to expect a different situation. In 1955 84 per cent of exports of farm implements made in Canada passed through United States ports. Likewise, 60 per cent of the automobiles exported and 49 per cent of automobile parts went via United States ports. Other products, where a greater or lesser proportion was involved, are such things as rubber tires, whisky, leather and electrical apparatus. Without exception, these commodities have the benefit of protection in the form of tariffs.
In other words, the Canadian consumer has to pay more for each of these articles he wants in order to enable them to be manufactured in Canada. Is it not reasonable then to suppose that the automobile industry, for example, show its appreciation of the protection it receives by directing foreign shipments from their plants through Canadian ports?
I should like to refer again to what I consider the need for permanent headquarters buildings for the army and air force in Halifax. I am not going to enlarge on that matter but I shall barely mention it. These services are operating in temporary buildings for the most part, and although I must commend both for the "spic and span" appearance of their buildings, there is still something to be desired.
The Address-Mr. Balcom
Last year in the house I expressed some views on the administration of the legislation concerning disability pensions. This forward step in our welfare program ought to have been received with general enthusiasm, but seldom has such a well-intentioned measure given me such concern.
Many people have complained of the rather rigid regulations and suggested a broader definition of total disability. This would doubtless solve many individual problems but it is not the whole answer. We must avoid putting a premium on being able to prove total disability, and the best way to do that is to provide an incentive for the individual to capitalize on any potential ability. This can be a broadly-conceived rehabilitation program which provides assistance and training for the people who are not totally and permanently disabled and for whom there is a chance of rehabilitation. An allowance should be paid for those people for whom there is some hope of rehabilitation, regardless of how meager that hope may be. Those who benefit from training and can make even a partial contribution to their own support will justify the program. This provision, with more flexibility in the general administration, would put the program where it should be.
Another measure in the field of social welfare which should be considered for revision is the Old Age Security Act. I believe it is time for an increase in the pensions paid to those over 70 and I suggest that another $10 per month be added. I realize that such an increase is in a sense contrary to the efforts of the government to curb inflation. However, I do not believe for a moment that the effect would be so serious as to outweigh the benefits. With a rising cost of living bearing so heavily on those who have not the capacity to increase their income to buy the necessities of life, we should be prepared to reconsider the needs of the aged. At the same time the assistance to the needy between 65 and 70 should also be boosted a similar amount. The inflationary impact on our economy would be more than offset or compensated for by the satisfaction in seeing these people happier in their last years.
In speaking of our social security, I should also like to suggest that there be reciprocity among commonwealth countries. We want an interchange of people. Especially do we want more immigrants from the United Kingdom. If we want to encourage this immigration we should be prepared to give such people the benefits of Canadian citizenship, namely the right to old age security without the limitation of 20-year residence. This could be done
72	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Balcom upon a reciprocal basis between Canada and the United Kingdom, and with other commonwealth countries which are willing to extend the same benefits.
There is another way in which the government can help to improve the position of the older age group and at the same time benefit the economy. This is in the application of its retirement policy. Automatic retirement at 65 does not make sense in the light of our present knowledge of the differing capacities of people at various ages. While it may not be quite true to say that you are as young as you feel, you can say that some feel and are much younger at 65 than others are at 55, and so on.
This is a situation in which the government should take the lead and not bring up the rear as it is doing at the present time. The employment policy of the civil service, and for that matter those who head up hourly-paid government employees, should be such as to utilize the services of people as long as they are willing and able to work. I know it is a great comfort to any civil servant-and to any politician for that matter-to have everything laid down by rule and regulation. Then when anyone comes along with a situation that calls for judgment, we can say that we have no discretion in the matter. However, that is a poor way in which to face up to the demands of a complicated society. Let us tackle these problems even though we are creating difficulties for ourselves. I am still convinced that it is better to be maligned and in the political wilderness and to have made a contribution to good government than to have overlooked problems for the sake of comfort and re-election.
I am asking at this time that all those hourly-paid and prevailing-rate employees who have reached the age of 65 or over, but under 70, and can do a day's work be retained in 1957. If necessary, have an independent commission or committee be the judge as to who is fit to continue.
On the employment practices of the government I have another matter to bring up. I refer to the practice of the civil service with regard to persons convicted of crimes. Here we are, as a government, spending substantial sums of money to train prisoners for jobs when they return to society. Our government spokesmen encourage such organizations as the John Howard Society to help in the rehabilitation of ex-prisoners. We ask private industry to employ people who have been convicted of crimes but have paid their penalties. We exhort private employers to give such people a chance to become useful members of society. How can


the government expect the public to take seriously its exhortations on penal reform and rehabilitation? Common humanity would suggest to an employer that he give the unfortunate a "leg up" instead of driving him into the streets. Let us get out from behind some of these comfortable rules and require the exercise of judgment in the name of humanity.
There are many other matters with which I should like to deal but I will not do so at this time. I refer to such matters as the formation of an independent parole board in Canada, and not only one but three in different parts of Canada so that they will be available and handy. I should like to speak on the world health organization, but I shall leave that till later. I should certainly like to say something about the salacious literature which is so prevalent in Canada. I should also like to speak about the evil of the trading and bonus stamps which are so prevalent at the present time. On a later occasion I should like to speak on the expeditious and happy way in which the customs branch, the immigration branch, the Red Cross and volunteer workers handled the influx of Hungarian refugees at Halifax on every occasion.
I should like to mention now, and perhaps speak later on it, the matter of a suggested change whereby the dominion sales tax would be collected at the wholesale level instead of the manufacturer's level. I wonder who thought that one up! It is not in the spirit of the first tax collector in the world, namely Saint Matthew. He was far too humane and understanding even to think of such an imposition.

The Address-Mr. Ellis

-and a rapidly increasing cost of living. I might say to the Minister of Finance that over the years the Regina Leader-Post, a newspaper in my own constituency, has always given support to the Liberal party. Just a month ago this newspaper stated it now agreed inflation has reached runaway proportions. I suggest that when such a strong champion of the Liberal party as the Regina Leader-Post now comes to this conclusion, the government should take some action to prevent this rapidly increasing cost of living.
There have been other evidences of that, Mr. Speaker. There is the failure of the government, in view of the increasing cost of living, to provide decent old age pensions; the failure of the government to make provision for increases in war veterans allowances or to make provision for others in this country on fixed incomes who are victimized by this runaway inflation. I think these are things which all members of this house must sincerely regret.
This morning some questions were asked of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) concerning the housing program in this country. I am always amazed at the Minister of Public Works because he uses these terms "housing starts" and "housing completions" interchangeably. A year or so ago if he were asked a question about housing in Canada he would say that next year we are going to have so many starts. This year when he is asked a question about how many starts have been made, he is now talking about completions. He will not admit that, while it is true completions have been high owing to starts made previously, as a result of the fiscal policies of this government home construction is falling off. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) states in his year end review, to which reference was made this morning, that in the Canadian economy the one segment which will suffer a significant decline is the home construction industry, then the government should take heed of this warning and do something to accelerate the housing program in this country.
The figures showing the amount of homes being constructed must be viewed in connection with the natural increase in our population and the fact that there are many new Canadians being welcomed to our shores. There is no excuse for any falling off of home construction in this country. There is a tremendous backlog of housing needs which should be met. Hon. members will recall 82715-6
Minister of Public Works whether, in view of the fact home construction starts were falling off-they are certainly falling off in my constituency and I fancy that is the general picture throughout Canada-the government might not be prepared to introduce some legislation to restore or to increase the number of homes being constructed in this country during the coming years. Of course, we get the answer again boasting of the number of completions which have been made and completely ignoring the fact that while a certain number of completions may have been made in the past year, the rate of home construction in Canada is falling off. There is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate the government is aware of these extremely important issues.
Now, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in a debate of this type we have some responsibility in bringing to the attention of the government the issues which we feel most important. I think that of all the immediate issues facing parliament at the present time, one of the most important is the suspension of rail operations on the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have this comment to make at the outset, that I can hardly conceive of any labour dispute which has occurred in Canada in recent years in which the general public has received so little information about one side of the case. I think it may be due to the fact that the public relations work of the railroad brotherhood has been a little weak and they have not been successful in getting their point of view across to the public. On the other hand, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has done a very good public relations job in getting across its side of the story.
We find newspaper editorials in which it is categorically stated that firemen helpers are not necessary; they take that as being the ultimate. On whose authority do they make this statement? It is made simply as a result of the submission made by the railroad company, without consideration to the excellent case put up by the railroad brotherhood. There have been comments made in the press and by the general public about the calling of this strike. There have been suggestions made that the rank and file membership of the brotherhood did not have a vote on this particular issue. These allegations completely ignore the fact that this matter was introduced almost a year ago.
It was on February 1 of last year that the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and engine-men approached the company to negotiate a

The Address-Mr. Ellis new contract. After negotiations had commenced-as a matter of fact, after negotiations had been in progress for a week or so- the Canadian Pacific Railway injected the issue of the diesel rule. In other words when the two parties to the contract negotiations were sitting around the table discussing the issues which were negotiable, the railway company saw fit to inject an issue which is extremely important, an issue which affects not only the members of the brotherhood but the safety of all Canadians.
When the Canadian Pacific Railway Company submitted its proposal to eliminate firemen helpers from diesel engines in freight and yard service, identical proposals were submitted by Canadian National Railways and by some 140 railroads in the United States. The second point to bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, is that later in the same year, as a matter of fact on November 20, the Canadian National Railways signed an agreement with the brotherhood as did the 140 railroads in the United States. When we state, therefore, that firemen are not necessary simply because Mr. Crump and the C.P.R. say so, then we must take into consideration the fact that the Canadian National Railways and 140 railways in the United States have seen fit to sign an agreement with the brotherhood providing for the retention of firemen helpers on diesels in freight and yard service. The question then arises, who is correct? Is the C.P.R. right and all the other railroads wrong? Is everybody out of step but the C.P.R.?
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At one o'clock the house took recess.
