speechtext:
When the house rose at one o'clock I was discussing the effectiveness of the company's propaganda in creating a climate of public opinion favourable to the railway company in connection with the present dispute between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen. I pointed out' that the Canadian public, on a technical matter of this kind, is perhaps not fully acquainted with all the details involved in the dispute and therefore is likely to be misled in any conclusions arrived at. I feel that the effectiveness of the railroad company's public relations campaign, coupled with the fact of having many friends in high places, indicates

one of the reasons why many of the newspapers in Canada are able to editorialize and create very misleading impressions about the nature of this dispute. I am quite sure that in this dispute we are very much disappointed with the action, or lack of action, taken by the government. I should have thought that the government would have used its good offices to promote an orderly settlement and perhaps to have averted this unfortunate stoppage of work on the C.P.R. Above all, I should have thought that the official opposition would have fulfilled their proper function and would have submitted some practical alternative. It could not be an alternative because the government had not made its wishes known; but certainly it could have given some advice to the government on how best to deal with this particular matter. But I understand that the Prime Minister has had in the past very close association with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in his capacity as a corporation lawyer.
Moreover, I know that the leader of the official opposition has on numerous occasions gone to bat on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I know that in the agricultural committee last year the Leader of the Opposition was very quick to jump to the defence of the C.P.R. and to describe that company as being made the scapegoat in connection with the distribution of box cars. Therefore, in the circumstances the reticence on the part of members of this house to seek to convey to the Canadian public the facts concerning this dispute is most regrettable. I have particular reference to a letter which was presumably drafted and sent to all employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company but which, in my judgment, was intended mainly to be used as a propaganda weapon directed against the general public. In that letter, a very plausible sounding letter, very well drafted and over the signature of the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, many misleading statements are made. Among the statements made by Mr. Crump is the one that there can be no dispute about firemen's wages or working conditions. The letter goes on to say:
The conciliation board recommended wage increases totalling 12 per cent-the same as agreed on with other train service employees-and extra pay for six statutory holidays in yard service.
Of course, the thing we have to bear in mind today is that what the railway company is going to do is to negotiate with a group on the basis that that group would liquidate itself, so that any talk about wage increases, of course, begs the main question. As far as there being no dispute is concerned, I would draw your attention to the fact that when the

union presented its proposals last' February 1 they asked for a 25 per cent wage increase, so that there is a reasonable dispute in connection with wages, but the major issue, of course, involves the diesel question.
I think I should point out at this time, Mr. Speaker, that in the United States the railway companies have signed a 3-year agreement with members of the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen calling for a general wage increase amounting to some 26J cents per hour. Therefore, I think I can rightly say there are many issues in dispute. But Mr. Crump points out that there is no dispute on those issues, and goes on to say:
There can be no dispute about firemen in passenger service. Passenger trains will continue to have firemen. The company proposes to run diesels without firemen only in freight and yard service. This will be a gradual change.
That is not what the Canadian Pacific Railway asked for in their submissions to the union and in their submissions to the conciliation board. As a matter of fact, the C.P.R. asked for the elimination of agreements, rules, regulations, interpretations or practices, however established, which require the employment or use of firemen helpers on other than steam power, and establish a rule to provide that the company shall have the unrestricted right to determine when and if a fireman helper shall be used on other than steam power. In other words, the C.P.R. says, we are not asking for that; it is not involved in this dispute; but in their submission before the conciliation board they asked for unlimited powers. The reason the Canadian Pacific Railway Company claim that they are not asking for the removal of firemen from diesels in passenger service is not that they are concerned about the safety of the travelling public, but rather that in order to heat the passenger cars it is necessary to have someone in the cab to take care of the steam generator. Therefore, there is no guarantee whatsoever that the railroad company might not at some future date use the unlimited powers which they are seeking, if they are granted, to remove firemen helpers from the diesels on passenger service. Then, Mr. Crump goes on and says:
There is no dispute about the jobs of any firemen who have worked three years or more. They will stay on as firemen until they become enginemen.
This sounds very good to the average person reading it. They might think these people are being well taken care of; but how on earth can you guarantee employment as firemen if there are no jobs as firemen? Anyone who knows anything about the operation of railroads knows very well that 82715-6J
The Address-Mr. Ellis runs are obtained on the basis of seniority, and if the railroad company is going to dismiss a thousand or more firemen almost immediately, then the chances of firemen getting employment at their trade are practically negligible. The only employment they are likely to obtain will be on steam service for the time being until the line is completely dieselized. Other advancements, of course, will be made possible only through the death or retirement of existing locomotive engineers. Therefore, this is somewhat meaningless when examined very closely.
Then, in similar vein, Mr. Crump goes on to point out:
Nor can there be any dispute about firemen with less than three years service. They are to get other jobs with Canadian Pacific and without loss of their seniority as firemen. If they desire to leave the service the company will pay them a cash allowance based on their length of service.
Here again this is entirely meaningless, because there will be no work for these men as firemen, and what is the use of seniority as firemen if there is no employment as firemen? I think these statements made by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company deserve some careful consideration by the people of Canada in order that justice might be done.
Then, the suggestion made by Mr. Crump that severance pay be granted is highly significant because, if firemen leave the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, it will not be because they desire to change their employment; it will be because they are virtually forced out of employment since there are no jobs as firemen.
There are statements with regard to diesels in passenger service. They say that there is no dispute, but at the same time the railway company is proposing that the firemen left in their employment on diesels in passenger service shall take about a 35 per cent reduction in salary. In spite of that, the railway company says there is no dispute. There is a great deal of dispute on every one of those principles, and yet the railway company is using big advertisements in every daily newspaper across Canada to give the public a very misleading idea of the issues involved in this dispute. As a result of this letter the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is seeking to do two things. First of all, he is trying to create the impression that no fireman in the employ of the company will suffer as a result of the acceptance of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's decision. I think the comments I have made give the lie to that assertion.
Furthermore, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, through this letter, are trying to convey the impression that the board of

The Address-Mr. Ellis conciliation came out solidly on their behalf. Mr. Speaker, I draw your attention to the fact that even in the majority report of the conciliation board, the board gave only conditional support to the position taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. As a matter of fact, in the summary of the conclusions arrived at by the conciliation board, they admit they have not considered this problem in its entirety. They state:
The board has not undertaken to discuss and analyze all the evidence tendered in support of and against the company's proposal for a change in the "diesel rule", but it has taken all the evidence both pro and con into consideration and has examined all the exhibits and has weighed carefully the submissions and arguments of counsel for the brotherhood and for the railway.
In other words, they have admitted that they have made no study of the technical aspects of this particular problem. They have simply listened to the opposing arguments of counsel representing the brotherhood on the one hand and the railway company on the other, and they have arrived at their conditional decision on the basis of arguments pro and con.
The majority report goes on to say:
The board's conclusion thus arrived at is that the company has established, in the main, its contention and accordingly we recommend that the company should be allowed to change the ''diesel rule" which would allow it to operate locomotives in freight and yard service without a fireman in the cab upon the understanding, however, that if as a result of actual operating experience it appears that in some circumstances the services of the fireman (helper) might again be required, a modification of the rule might again be necessary and would then become the subject of further bargaining at a time when another agreement is being negotiated.
So that it gives conditional support. They said, "Let us try it out for a year and if it does not work out we will go back". If the safety factor is involved, is it not wiser to make sure there is no danger to the travelling public or to the employees of the railway company before making the change? Surely this is preferable to making the change and then waiting until there is a major train accident involving the loss of life and limb and personal property before the railway company recognizes the lack of wisdom in seeking to force this issue at the present time.
The majority report is by no means absolute in its support of the contentions of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. And let us also consider the minority report. There is no more forthright denunciation of the proposals of the railway company than are contained in the report submitted by Senator Roebuck. In his minority report Senator Roebuck makes an excellent case on behalf of the people of Canada because there is more involved in this dispute than the question of

the employment of a thousand odd firemen on the Canadian Pacific Railway. What is involved is the question of whether the railway company shall be permitted to take an action which will jeopardize the safety of the travelling public; that is the main issue.
In my own constituency my own children cross railway tracks on their way to school every day and this is true of many children in every city in Canada. Children being what they are they will play around switching yards. The railways are unable to fence off their property and ensure that the safety of pedestrian traffic and particularly children is protected and guaranteed at all times. I would hate to think of any children playing around railway yards where one side of the locomotives is blind, where there is no man on the left side of the locomotive. I believe this is something which should be of concern to each and every parent and citizen of this country.
If the railway proposal goes through and the second man is taken out of the cabs of locomotives in yard service going back and forth on to spare tracks it will be done only at the expense of jeopardizing the safety of the men, women and children who live in the vicinity of railway yards. Those are factors which the conciliation board admits it did not have the opportunity to examine in minute detail and that is the consideration the railway unions want to have examined in the minutest detail.
In examining the issues involved in this dispute I think one must consider the problem of the firemen themselves and the unsatisfactory assurances given by the railway company. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the majority report lays a certain amount of blame on the shoulders of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Concerning alternative employment for firemen the majority report at page 3 says:
If the company had seen fit to accompany its proposal on the diesel issue with a concrete blueprint, spelling out in detail what provision it was willing to make for the 1,000 odd firemen who would be immediately cut off the payroll, and the not inconsiderable number of other firemen who would ultimately lose their employment if the company request were granted, the no compromise position which the union throughout maintained might have been at least in some respects relaxed or modified.
I think it is clear from what I have read that the majority report lays a great deal of the blame squarely on the shoulders of the railway company for not being more forthright and specific in its proposal to take care of the firemen who will be removed from employment, but as I have already indicated the major issue is the safety factor.

I can think of no better indication of the type of evidence presented before the conciliation board than that which can be gained by examining the type of witnesses who appeared before that board. Approximately 15 witnesses appeared on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway company and all of those people were executives. All but two of them were officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company primarily interested, of course, in safeguarding the interests of the shareholders of the company and inclined, of course, to place that consideration above all others. We know that as far as the union witnesses were concerned the brotherhoods brought in approximately 35 witnesses. Onjy two of their witnesses were foremen or men in supervisory work. All the other witnesses were men actually engaged in railroad operations including conductors, trainmen, brake-men and shop mechanics. All of these people gave evidence to the effect that in their opinion the removal of firemen from diesel locomotives could not be done without endangering the lives of both railroad employees and the general public.
It seems to me under that weight of evidence a strong case has been made for deferring any action on the question of the removal of firemen from diesel locomotives. It is also apparent to me that the locomotive engineers would perhaps have a more intimate knowledge of the role played by firemen and they have taken an unequivocal stand on this particular issue. They appeared before the conciliation board and pleaded with it to retain the firemen on diesel engines. Moreover, if you noticed the press report in one of the Toronto papers the other night you will be aware that the locomotive engineers in that city have stated categorically that irrespective of what might come of this dispute they are not prepared to take diesel locomotives out of the shops unless they are accompanied in the cab by a qualified fireman.
I believe that is a reasonable position for these men to take. They are the people best qualified to speak about the role played by firemen in diesel service. I think perhaps the terminology could be changed and firemen could better be described as co-engineers or assistant engineers. I think that is something which would go a long way toward eliminating some of the misunderstandings which presently exist.
It seems to me that we have to take into account the valued opinions of these people who are vitally concerned with railroad operations when coming to a conclusion on this broad issue. If everyone in Canada were in a position to read the excellent report submitted by Senator Roebuck the ground swell of public opinion would certainly be
The Address-Mr. Ellis solidly behind the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen. In that report Senator Roebuck makes it quite clear that in the interests of the safety of the travelling public and the railway employees themselves it is absolutely necessary to maintain in the cab of diesel locomotives fireman-helpers. Reference is made to the fact that T.C.A. planes have co-pilots and I suppose it might be argued that one pilot could handle the controls of the plane.
We have to recognize today that dieseliza-tion has made it possible for the railway companies to run more trains, longer trains and faster trains. This of course only points out the need for increased vigilance. Now is certainly not the time to be taking out of the cabs enginemen whose judgment is extremely necessary in many cases.
I think Senator Roebuck sums it up very well in his report when he refers to the tremendous responsibility placed upon the shoulders of the locomotive engineer. On page 3 of his report he points out:
There are few workers in the industrial life of Canada who bear so terrible a responsibility as that of the locomotive engineer in charge of a modern train.
And again:
So long as trains have been running, the engineer has been furnished with an assistant, who, in addition to taking care of the mechanical needs of the locomotive and sharing the task of lookout, has been charged with the responsibility of observance of the operating rules and the train orders and has kept track of changing schedules and has calculated the time of meets. The fireman is the engineer's co-pilot. It is not given to mere humans individually to always be right, to never be mistaken, and it is the duty and function of the fireman to catch an oversight, a momentary failure to observe, or a miscalculation of the time of an approaching train or the speed under varying conditions of his own train on the part of the engineer, and thus to avoid what would otherwise result in some frightful accident in which two trains may be involved with hundreds of thousands of dollars m property and the life and limb of passengers and crews.
That is a most categorical statement by one member of the conciliation board who makes it quite clear that in his view the position of the railway company is very ill-advised. It seems to me that some effort has been made to suggest that the firemen are holding out against automation. May I point out that dieselization already has cost almost 3,000 employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company their jobs and there was no sign of a work stoppage. Those people accepted the inevitable technological changes. Those mechanics in the shops were replaced by the dieselization program of the C.P.R.
As a result of dieselization the C.P.R. has been able to effect very considerable savings. According to their own figures, in

The Address-Mr. Ellis 1955 they saved some $18 million in transportation costs and an additional $6 million in the reduced maintenance of locomotives. One can therefore point out that dieselization already has brought about great savings to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. No one takes issue with that fact. We are happy to see these technical changes taking place.
What is involved here is not a question of automation, it is a question of the safety of the public generally and of the train crews.
It seems to me that in this dispute, which I hope will be speedily resolved, we should recognize the validity of the position taken by the brotherhood. The brotherhood's argument is quite clear. They say that the conciliation board should have been armed with sufficient technical knowledge in order to bring down an opinion based on more than a refereeing between two conflicting points of view. Reference was made this morning by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), to the fact that the three members of the conciliation board were lawyers. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) could not see anything wrong with that, but I suggest that if we are going to have an objective study made of this problem we will have to have experts and not lawyers consider it. Lawyers may be quite learned in the law but when it comes to operating a railway I think we should have the opinions of people who know what they are discussing. Certainly that cannot be achieved with the type of conciliation board referred to previously.
I am hoping that the Prime Minister's statement today presages a breaking of the stalemate and the bringing about of an early resumption of the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Clearly the position which the union has taken is quite logical and reasonable. They say that they are prepared to go back to work provided there is an undertaking that this matter will be referred to a board qualified to discuss the whole question and that the findings of that board will then be referred to a conciliation board.
The conciliation board to which we referred earlier admitted that it was not in a position to pass judgment on technical matters. The members of that board admitted that their judgment was based merely on the ability of the opposing counsel to put across the best point of view. Surely that is not the basis upon which an important matter of this kind should be settled.
I feel that the government has been lax in dealing with this matter. They have held over the heads of the employees the

threat of compulsory arbitration. The example of 1950 is still fresh in their minds. At the same time the government has not paid the slightest attention to the reasonable proposal put forth by the leader of this group the other day when he suggested that in the interests of the railroad workers themselves and in the interests of the Canadian people there should be an immediate resumption of rail operations over the lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and that if the railroad company was adamant in its refusal to meet that reasonable request the government should appoint an administrator to take over the temporary management of the C.P.R. and to see that the railroad trains are running as soon as possible.
I think that is the position as it stands at the moment. Negotiations are in progress and it is our earnest hope that the resumption of rail operations will occur at the earliest possible moment. I plead with the government to leave no stone unturned to see that the railway company are persuaded to adopt a proposal such as the one outlined by the Prime Minister today when he suggested that if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were prepared to accept the same settlement as that granted by Canadian National Railways while this matter was being investigated there was no reason why railroad operations could not be resumed. I suggest that the failure to come to a settlement must be placed squarely on the shoulders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Every effort should be made to bring about a resumption of rail operations. The onus now rests upon the railway company.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me particular pleasure this afternoon to extend the customary congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, not only because they made excellent speeches, well thought out, well composed and well delivered, but also because of the fact that they both spoke in the two official languages of our nation. I was particularly impressed by the fact that the mover, whose mother tongue is English, was able to speak to us at such length and so well in the French language. I was also impressed by the fact that the seconder, whose mother tongue is French, was able to speak to us at such length and so well in the English language. I congratulate these two members and at the same time I also wish to congratulate all members on both sides of the house who have been making the sincere effort that I have had occasion to observe during the last eight years to become more and more bilingual and to be able to understand and express themselves in the two official languages of our nation.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal with two of the subjects that are covered in the speech from the throne, the references to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the railway strike. Then I intend to discuss certain matters that concern my constituency particularly. In connection with NATO I find this reference in the speech from the throne:
An encouraging advance is being made, as evidenced by the latest ministerial meeting of the council, in the development of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in the non-military as well as in the military field. My ministers remain strongly convinced of the need to maintain the North Atlantic treaty as the keystone of the defence of the western nations.
Farther on I find this reference:
Recent events have confirmed my ministers' belief in the importance of seeking solutions to international problems through the United Nations and of upholding by all practical and constructive means the principles of the United Nations charter. My ministers also believe, however-
This is the part I wish to emphasize.
-that while making every effort to achieve these long term goals, the western nations must remain strong and united in their defences and in their diplomacy in order that aggressive action against them will be prevented and international tension can be lessened.
That paragraph evidently refers to NATO. As chairman of the executive committee of the Canadian NATO parliamentary association, I am of course pleased with these references to NATO made in the speech
The Address-Mr. Cannon from the throne and I heartily endorse the attitude that the government is taking. I had the privilege of leading the Canadian delegation to the interparliamentary conference that took place in Paris from the 18th to the 23rd of November last, and I think that the best way for me to express to the house my thoughts and feelings about the importance of NATO at this time is to quote from a speech that I delivered at this conference of NATO parliamentarians. I said:
When we were in Paris last year in the month of July the Geneva conference was taking place and the Russians were advancing their plans for peaceful coexistence putting on the mask of friendship and trying to give the impression that a great change had taken place in Russia since Stalin's death and that Russian policy was being liberalized, becoming more human and friendly. The Russian delegates to the Geneva conference declared their peaceful intentions and made disarmament proposals.
One of the main consequences of this attitude taken by the Russians was to make some people doubt the necessity and utility of NATO and to bring to some governments of NATO countries the temptation to reduce their efforts to build up NATO's military defence forces in Europe.
Some extreme optimists even expressed the view that before long NATO would no longer be so necessary and that the NATO countries would soon be able to diminish considerably if not abolish entirely their defence expenditures.
But, Mr. Chairman, what a change now! The deplorable events that have taken place in Hungary recently have altered all that.
The Russians when confronted by the courageous demands of the Hungarian people for self-government, for free elections, for the abolition of the farce that is the system of one-party elections and for the withdrawal of the Russian army from their country, showed their real nature; they removed the mask of hypocrisy and duplicity they had been wearing and gave free course to the brutality and the cruelty that have always been the hallmark of all communist regimes and particularly of the Soviet regime.
After having received the demands of the brave Hungarian people, they pretended to negotiate the withdrawal of Russian troops from the country. During the so-called negotiations and directly contrary to the object of these negotiations, they brought into Hungary great numbers of men and quantities of military equipment, forged a ring of steel composed of 1,000 tanks around Budapest and made prisoners the legitimate government of the country and the very envoys with whom they were supposed to be negotiating.
They then proceeded to drown in a bath of blood the protests and resistance of the Hungarian patriots.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this unmasking of the Russians has greatly changed the NATO picture.
There can no more be any doubt of the usefulness of NATO and the necessity of keeping defence forces strong and alert. There can be no doubt about the desirability of closer union between the different NATO countries and of tightening the cultural and economic bonds that unite them as foreseen by Article II of the treaty.
Those are my feelings, Mr. Speaker, about NATO, and I am pleased that so many members of the Senate and the House of Commons have shown their interest in NATO by joining our association. The importance of NATO

The Address-Mr. Cannon parliamentary associations has been underlined and I think there should be placed on the record an excerpt from the report of the committee of three, of which our distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was one, which was appointed by NATO to make a report. Their report has been issued recently, and paragraphs 58 and 59 of the report read as follows:
58.	Among the best supporters of NATO and its purposes are those members of parliament who have had a chance at first hand to see some of its activities and to learn of its problems, and to exchange views with their colleagues from other parliaments. In particular, the formation of national parliamentary associations and the activities of the conference of members of parliament from NATO countries have contributed to the development of public support for NATO and solidarity among its members.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that is a very interesting and, in my opinion, very well deserved commendation of NATO parliamentary associations on the part of the members of this committee of three. They go on to say:
59.	In order to maintain a close relationship of parliamentarians with NATO, the following arrangements are recommended:
(a)	That the Secretary-General continue to place the facilities of NATO headquarters at the disposal of parliamentary conferences and give all possible help with arrangements for their meetings.
(b)	That invited representatives of member governments and the Secretary-General and other senior NATO civil and military officers attend certain of these meetings. In this way the parliamentarians would be informed on the state of the alliance and the problems before it, and the value of their discussions would be increased.
I submit you have there, Mr. Speaker, a very useful and very interesting appraisal of the importance of associations such as ours. By chance, and purely by chance, our meeting in Paris in the month of November came at a very opportune time. I say by chance because, of course, the date of the conference had been fixed many weeks or months before the Suez canal difficulties arose and before, as a result of those difficulties and the events about which we all know, a certain division arose among the three principal, original members of NATO, namely, England, France and the United States. I say that our meeting was particularly well timed because it gave an opportunity to parliamentarians of the free countries to meet to discuss their differences of opinion, to thresh out the matter, I might say. I am convinced that these meetings, these conversations, these arguments if you like, did a great deal of good and helped to bring together the opinions of parliamentarians of these three countries.
The fundamental importance of the NATO parliamentary associations was brought home to us in 1955 by no less a personage than General Gruenther. When we went to

supreme headquarters, SHAPE, in Paris General Gruenther gave us a briefing. One of the things he said to us was this. He said we must not forget that all the members of the North Atlantic treaty alliance are democracies and that in a democracy the very existence of the government depends upon public opinion. Therefore in a democracy a continuance of the policy of any government depends equally upon public opinion. If we wish NATO to continue to endure and to continue to give to the freedom-loving nations the service that it is giving, he said, we must interest public opinion in the NATO countries in NATO and the work that NATO is doing; and, said General Gruenther, the best way in which to interest public opinion in NATO and the work that NATO is doing is to get parliamentarians who are the representatives of the people, who are the representatives of public opinion in their different countries, interested in NATO; and the best way in which to do that is to organize NATO parliamentary associations in the different countries.
The Canadians who attended this meeting took an active part. Out of 14 members of the Canadian delegation there were seven speakers. Those speakers were the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Leduc), the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Holling-worth), the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) and myself. In proportion to the numbers of our delegation, I think that we had one of the best records. I do not think that any delegation had more than 50 per cent of their members making speeches. I say this to underline what an active interest our delegates took in the proceedings. While I am on this subject I wish to mention the fact that the two delegates sent by the Senate distinguished themselves. Senator McLean was elected head of the economic committee. Senator Dessureault took an active part in the deliberations of the political committee.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we came back from this meeting of NATO parliamentarians in time for the short session which was called here in November to deal with the Suez matter. My experience at NATO confirmed this year the opinion that I had formed last year and convinced me more than ever of the necessity and the utility of these NATO parliamentary associations and their meetings.
I now pass on to the second subject with which I wish to deal and which is alluded to in the speech from the throne. I refer to the railway strike. I do not pretend to be an expert-far from it-and I have not gone

into the pros and cons of the matter. I am not going to express my opinion as to whether the railway company is right or whether the union is right. I am going to examine the subject from the point of view of the general public. From the point of view of the general public I must say that I think these strikes in public utilities are extremely deplorable indeed. I have had some experience in the matter because in 1950 I was privileged to move the address in reply to the speech from the throne in the special session that took place that year for the purpose of dealing with the disastrous railway strike when both of our railways were strikebound. I wish to quote briefly from a speech I made on that occasion. Dealing with strikes in public utilities I had this to say as reported at page 84 of Hansard of August 31, 1950:
In the province of Quebec, public opinion has already accepted legislation forbidding strikes in public utilities. In 1944. the legislative assembly of that province passed a bill decreeing compulsory arbitration in every dispute over labour conditions where a public utility and its employees were involved and rendering illegal any strike in a public utility under any circumstances whatsoever.
Heavy penalties are provided in this legislation for every day that such an illegal strike would last. This law is still in force and has given good results. It was enacted by a Liberal government known for its sympathy towards organized labour.
However our federal government did not want to incorporate this principle into the labour legislation of this country. It did not want to enact general legislation prohibiting strikes in public utilities and subjecting them to compulsory arbitration.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether public opinion is not coming around now to that idea, now that we have had another railway strike within six years. I wonder whether public opinion would not accept legislation outlawing strikes in public utilities, based, of course, on the general principle that the general good must be given preference over the good of the individual or even over the good of a group of individuals. I do not wish to elaborate on the matter now but I wish to leave with the house the thought that three things might help in the future to avoid in railways and in public utilities strikes that are so detrimental to the economy and to the well-being of our country. Apart from legislation prohibiting strikes in public utilities there is also the thought that if there was less influence by outside unions on our unions in Canada, there might be fewer labour disturbances. If our unions were entirely independent and were not subject to the influence of other branches of so-called international unions, I think that situation might also help to avoid strikes. In the third place, I think that the method of voting on such important issues is surprising, to say the least. I was greatly surprised to read in the
The Address-Mr. Cannon editorial of a newspaper-it is a well-informed paper and I have no reason to believe that what was stated is not true-that this strike which we are now suffering was decided by a vote of 36 men sent by telegraph, namely the 36 heads of the different unions that were involved. The workmen were never given the chance to vote. The workmen were never given the chance to declare themselves as to whether or not they wanted to strike. The thought that I am going to leave-

You make your own speech some time. The thought I wish to express is this. If legislation were passed to oblige that a secret ballot be taken of all workmen affected by a strike, it might have a considerable effect in avoiding strikes of this kind in the future.
These are three suggestions that I make. I am sure that they will not all be adopted by the government at the same time but I am making them nonetheless and I underline these suggestions. Even if only one of these three suggestions were adopted, it might have a considerable effect in avoiding strikes of the kind from which we are now suffering.

Mr. Speaker, I am now coming to the part of my speech which deals with the fine county of the Magdalen islands, which I have the honour to represent in this house.
First, I wish to thank, in the name of my constituents, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and all those who helped secure President Eisenhower's rejection of the recommendation which had been made by the United States tariff board, suggesting the imposition of an additional duty on the importation of Canadian fish to the United States. If that resolution had been sanctioned by the president of the United States, it would have had disastrous effects on Canada's eastern fisheries and particularly on the Magdalen islands fisheries, inasmuch as a large part of their products are marketed in the United States. Therefore, in the name of my constituents, I should like to express my most sincere appreciation to the right hon. Prime Minister and to all others who appealed to President Eisenhower in this respect.
In the name of my constituents, I also want more particularly to thank the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) for having authorized the fine modern airport, which is already in operation on Magdalen islands. Until now,

The Address-Mr. Cannon aircraft have had to land on the beach, which was at times fairly easy to do, but at other times not quite so easy. I am proud to say we obtained the building of this airport because conditions on the beach were not always the best. While I am on the subject of aviation, I want also to seize the opportunity of thanking the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lapointe) for giving us a daily mail delivery service. When I was first elected member for the Magdalen islands, we had only semi-weekly mail service. Some time ago, I had managed to obtain three weekly deliveries. Now, with the co-operation of the Postmaster General and the Maritime Central Airways, we too will enjoy a daily service.
The year 1956 was a good year for us. Our fisheries yielded about twice as much as in 1954. I do not intend to claim any credit for that increase, since it is due to the fact that fishing was better or that our fishermen were luckier. Besides, if I were to take credit for it, I would have to take the blame when fishing is bad, and everyone knows that the result of fishing is always rather uncertain.
However, I am convinced that the improvements made at the Iles-de-la-Madeleine these last eight years, improvements to the ports, the harbours and wharves, the slips which have been installed, the breakwaters which have been put up, the dredging which has been done to improve shipping, as well as the assistance given towards shipbuilding and the buying of equipment for our fishermen, have greatly helped my people to achieve these splendid results. That is why, finding that the value of the catch by the Magdalen islands fishermen in 1956 was twice as large as in 1954, I want to thank the government most sincerely for what they have done for my county.
I now come to unemployment insurance. Ever since I have been the member for the Magdalen islands-it will be eight years next summer-I have, at each session, untiringly asked for the payment of unemployment insurance to fishermen. At the last session of parliament, my efforts were successful, thanks to the understanding of the government and, more particularly, of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). Through an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act, fishermen came under the act. Regulations are now being prepared which will apply to those cases, and which, I am told, will come into force not later than next April. Fishermen will then benefit from the act on the same basis as workers in other industries. There, again, is a great improvement for the fishermen of Magdalen islands.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a few words now on the subject of family allowances. My views on this matter I have stated in this house on previous occasions. I shall therefore limit myself to quoting from a speech 1 made January 17, 1956, on the occasion of this same debate in reply to the speech from the throne. Talking about family allowances, I said:
Our great leader, the late Right Hon. W. L-Mackenzie King, was responsible for them and history will record that his decision to create family allowances was that of a great statesman.
But over ten years have gone by and family allowances have not been increased. As everyone knows, the cost of living has increased enormously during that time, while the needs of children have not decreased. The means of meeting the needs of the children should be increased to keep pace with the cost of supplying them.
Then I said further:
I have received representations, both verbally and in writing, from my constituents to the effect that they think it is time family allowances were increased. These people point to the increase in the cost of living since 1945 and the fact that government income available for purposes other than war purposes has greatly increased since that time. I agree with them, and I make an appeal to the government to increase family allowances. If they cannot double them, as requested in some quarters, they should at least increase them 25 per cent or 50 per cent. If it is impossible for the government to increase family allowances all along the line they should-and this is the minimum they should do-at least increase the monthly allowances of $5, $6 or $7 for the younger children to the J8 given to the older children, so the same scale would apply to all. This modification would not only benefit the children but would greatly simplify the administration of the act.
Such were my sentiments last year, Mr. Speaker, and such are they again this year. My constituents send me many representations, signed by hundreds of my good friends, people who admire the government and the right hon. Prime Minister, and who, despite the improvement with which they have been gratified and the good things they have received from the government, keep writing me to ask that family allowances be increased. I believe those requests are justified, and for the same reasons as were put forward by myself last year I say again that family allowances should be increased.
I would go even further and say, that, in my belief, family allowances are more important than health insurance. All people have children who need education, clothing and food; but not everyone becomes ill. I sincerely believe that it is more important to increase family allowances than to provide for health insurance.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize the fact that unemployment insurance benefits paid to Magdalen islands fishermen will put several hundred thousand

dollars into circulation in this constituency. The estimate I have been given amounts to four or five hundred thousand dollars, and this will help our fishermen to get by until family allowances are increased. While I point out this fact, I none the less urge an increase of family allowances as soon as possible.
In the matter of public works, I should like to mention very briefly the main projects that should be undertaken in the Magdalen islands. To give an idea of the needs in the western end of the islands, I need only quote an article from the magazine A Pleines Voiles which is published at Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere and is interested especially in the welfare of fishermen. That magazine prints a column entitled "The Voice of the Islands" which I always read very carefully. I need not mention that the islands referred to are the Magdalen islands. Any Madelinot knows that when one refers to "the islands," one always means the Magdalen Islands. I quote:
Grande-Entree is up and coming!
At the south of Grande-Entree lies the lie du Bassin. Between it and Grande-Entree, the sea forms a marvelous little bay, sheltered from the winds, east and west, by the sand banks. If it were adequately developed, that bay could be turned into the best fishing harbour of the islands; it would be mostly suitable for all kinds of fishing, especially for lobster, halibut and cod. The required works would include the digging of a channel on the west side and the construction of a protective wall, docks and factories. Thus, the eastern part of the islands would be saved for fisheries and would enjoy the prospect of a most promising economic future.
Such is the project advocated by the religious and civil authorities of Grande-Entree and by the taxpayers of that community. Such is the foremost proposition at the present time at the islands and everybody is in favour of it.
I spoke about it to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). I am sure that he is interested in that project and I am confident that work will be undertaken this very year in order that this marvelous project may be implemented at Grande-Entree.
Mr. Speaker, here are a few among the public works which will be undertaken at the islands and which are included in my program. A new breakwater at North Cape (Cap-du-Nord), a new breakwater at Dune-du-Sud to prevent silting, such as has been the case with the present structure, improvements to the harbours at Pointe-Basse and Cap-aux-Meules, construction of a quay or dock on the west side of l'Etang-du-Nord.
As regards harbour improvements at Havre-Aubert, the chamber of commerce there recently prepared a blueprint, a copy of which was sent to me and which I have forwarded to the Minister of Public Works.
The Address-Mr. Cannon I am sure that department officials will find it most useful in planning future work at Havre-Aubert. I also take this opportunity to congratulate the members of the Havre-Aubert chamber of commerce on the spirit of initiative and of public duty they have shown in preparing this plan and in sending me a copy.
We also have an airport at Havre-Aubert, although not as large as the one built at Havre-aux-Maisons, to which I referred a moment ago. However, and precisely because it is a smaller one, it should be enlarged, maintained and improved. The reason is evident. Business is picking up at Havre-Aubert, as everywhere else in the islands, and it would not be fair to let this airport go to ruin. I have already asked the Department of Transport to enlarge it, and I will keep on asking that this be done. I am sure my good friend the Minister of Transport will admit that my representations are well founded.
We also wish to improve the wharf and the slip at Entry island and to deepen the harbour at Etang-des-Caps.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a short summary of what we in the Magdalen islands would require in the way of works for this year. I am sure that the government will favourably consider these requests which I am submitting.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of these few remarks, I have dealt with matters in the international, national and local fields. I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister for the important part he played in world affairs thanks to his friendly contacts with such people as the president of the United States, Mr. Eisenhower, and Mr. Nehru, the prime minister of India. It is a great satisfaction to our people to see that we can rely on the firm and sure guidance of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Liberal government in these particularly difficult times on the international level. Clearly the people of Canada are also very satisfied with their government, at the national level, and I am sure that new evidence of this satisfaction will be given by a resounding victory of our beloved leader and our party at the next general election. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising today to take part in this throne speech debate I, like those before me, wish to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud). To the mover I just wish to say that I enjoyed very much the remarks that he had to make, and I regret
84	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. H. O. White that I was unable to follow the speech of the seconder, but I did take the time to read it.
Each session of parliament each year, Mr. Speaker, seems to bring its particular problems, and this year of 1957, only in its 10th day, seems to be loaded with problems, even though the announcement expected today of the settlement of the strike will bring some measure of relief to many thousands of Canadians. It seems to me there are five problems that loom large on the horizon of 1957 in its 365-day run. I do, however, wish to say a word or two about the strike, and not only this strike but what might and could be done for the future. One other item of immense importance is the state of international affairs, with the Middle East the hot spot and the Kremlin engaged in making trouble wherever it seems to be possible or profitable for them so to do.
Another problem facing Canadians is that of inflation. We have heard a great deal about it. Much has been said about it in the 10 years since the war. There is also the problem of agriculture, the poor relations in a booming economy, and our $1 billion trade deficit, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) says is an indication of the growth and development of this country.
Yesterday, the Prime Minister, in his speech dealing with the problems of the day, revealed the mailed fist in the gloved hand, and today the strike is more or less settled. All Canadians are alarmed at the recurring number of strikes and are asking for and thinking that there must be, some solution to the problems of relations between industry and labour, not only on the railways but in many key industries. They are alarmed at the influence exerted by persons outside of Canada in these labour troubles. They are also alarmed at the control outside of Canada of many of our key industries and raw resources.
I think the search on the part of hon. members of parliament for a solution not only to the rail strike which is concluding but concerning the question of strikes in major industries generally is an indication of the importance which they feel strikes assume in relation to the economy of the country and how they can cripple a nation if of long duration or extended to more than one or two industries in the country. The worst feature of such strikes is the fact that in many cases the innocent bystander is injured to a greater extent than is the industry or the men involved.
If a strike progresses the supplying industries become idle either through lack of raw 

materials or lack of markets and we find even today that as a result of the strike lumber, mining, manufacturing and agriculture all have been seriously affected. But the worst effect, in my estimation, is on the small businessman who lacking the resources of large corporations is not able to withstand the blow of the strike and in a short time faces economic disaster.
I am wondering if it would be possible for us, in regard to industrial strife, to apply our thinking as far as international affairs are concerned. Hon. members will recall that at the close of the first world war of 1914-18 there was set up at that time a league of nations and although it collapsed the idea and the ideal was to prevent an outbreak of another world war. If the United States had been prepared to play its part at that time the second world war might possibly have been averted. At the conclusion of the second world war in 1945 the nations got together again and set up the United Nations in the hope that it might avert a third world war.
In all democratic countries and in other countries, too, there are ethics, codes and laws which govern the relationship between man and man and for the settlement of civil disputes. Two parties engage in a lawsuit which goes to the courts and a judgment is handed down which is accepted as final and is enforced.
Similarly we have rules governing the field of sports. If we go to a ball game, a hockey match or a prize fight we accept the decisions which are made by the referee according to the rules of the game or the laws governing the sport. We have tried to achieve the same thing in the field of international affairs and possibly we have succeeded to a degree, but when it comes to the relationships between an employer and an employee we find we still have to slug it out until one side or the other succumbs or the government steps in. Whenever the government steps in it puts labour in a most unfortunate position because it leaves industry in the position where it can sit back and let the strike run its course in full confidence that the government will eventually intervene and end the strike. That is what we and labour generally do not wish to see come to pass in this country. Surely if we have developed to the stage where we have a tribunal for international disputes, civil law courts for the settlement of civil disputes and referees enforcing the laws governing the field of sports, disputes between labour and management can also be eliminated if the proper procedures could be brought into being which had the full confidence of labour and management and the Canadian people so that when a judgment was handed down

the weight of public opinion would make it almost necessary that the judgment be accepted by both parties.
For many years I have said in this house and outside of it that one of the solutions to industrial strife would be the introduction of profit sharing plans whereby labour becomes a partner with industry and shares in the wealth that the hands of labour have helped to create. It is interesting to note that more and more industries are adopting properly established profit sharing plans which are being enjoyed by many working people. Some companies have built up enormous resources for distribution to their employees. The strange thing about it, however, is that the leaders of unions are not interested in selling to employees the idea of profit sharing plans. They apparently seem to thrive on a certain amount of industrial strife. I hope, therefore, that before another serious strike is on our doorstep concrete action will be taken by labour and industry to avert such a disaster.
I wish to say a few words concerning our $1,000 million trade deficit and about trade in general. I noticed in the Prime Minister's speech yesterday he referred to the trade deficit and he used as a comparison a Canadian farmer who in the springtime would buy seed, feed and fertilizer and then in the fall would be able to make up his investment with the crop that he garnered. Our trade deficit is somewhat different and I am afraid a parallel such as the Prime Minister suggests cannot be drawn. We are buying this $1,000 million deficit from the United States of America but when the crop is harvested are we going to be able to sell it back to them? I do not believe it is possible. The United States is being very careful to see that any attempts made to sell our goods to that country are met with irritation, restrictions, uncertainties, give-away programs and a disregard for the GATT treaties. Consequently the easy solution suggested by the Prime Minister is not practical.
I also found it interesting to observe that it has been only during the last few weeks that the Prime Minister has become so acutely interested in the problem of the farmer and I am wondering if the proximity of an election has had some effect on his thinking as far as agriculture is concerned.
The argument is being advanced that we must buy from abroad in order to sell abroad, but the joker in the pack, so far as that argument is concerned, is this. Canada is a great producing nation, yet we are buying a great many agricultural products from abroad, products which we as Canadians
The Address-Mr. H. O. White could produce. Those products purchased abroad provide dollars with which foreign countries are able to buy Canadian manufactured products. They do not buy Canadian farm products. Actually the Canadian farm economy is being exploited to provide markets for manufactured goods.
There is another disturbing factor as far as agriculture is concerned and that is that in this inflated, high-cost economy we are being undersold by many countries. Our industries are protected by tariffs while many farm products are protected only for short periods of time, in some cases for as little as three weeks. I wonder why this is being done. I should not wonder because I think I know the answer. This government has found by experience through several elections that between elections they can kick the farmer around but when the next election rolls around the farmer will still vote for them.
It is interesting to note and I mention it again that yesterday and recently the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) dealt with agricultural problems. It is interesting to note that the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and others have been quoting statistics to prove how well off agriculture is, but I want to say to the government that agricultural statistics are not negotiable, they do not pay taxes, they do not buy feed, seed and fertilizer nor do they pay the interest on the mortgage. If they did, our farmers would be tickled to death because they would be able to get along. But the fact is that agricultural statistics do none of those things.
I was interested also in what the Prime Minister had to say about his golf game. He seemed to be able to improve his golf score and his social relations with the President of the United States but apparently he was not able to reduce the $1,000 million trade deficit by any appreciable degree.

While I am dealing with our trade problems I should like to say a little about the problem of inflation. For many years Canadians have been led to believe that the Bank of Canada by controlling currency and credit controlled the bank rate, but now when the issue is becoming a hot one we see news items in the papers and otherwise stating that the bank rate is controlled by the sale of treasury bills as they are bid for and sold each Friday. But they fail to tell you that while the chartered banks, brokerage firms and others can buy and sell treasury bills, the Bank of Canada is also in the market and can control the bank interest rate while saying to the public that they have nothing to do with it.
I might mention for the information of the house that I called up the Bank of Canada this morning and tried to get hold of one of these treasury bills. They told me that they were easily negotiable and were worth from $25,000 right up to $1 million. They did not provide me with one but they told me what they looked like.

No, I did not
buy one. The average Canadian is asking who is fooling whom about this bank rate and is the increased bank rate likely to do the things it is proposed it will do as far as inflation is concerned. We have been told, and I think I am prepared to believe it, that inflation can be brought about in two ways. It can be brought about by a surplus of money-I do not know of any farmer in Ontario or anywhere else who would know anything about a surplus of money-or by an undersupply or scarcity of goods. By making it more difficult for businesses to carry on, an increased interest rate becomes part of the cost of goods sold. Industry is discouraged from producing and this brings about a further scarcity of goods rather than making them more plentiful. I cannot see how the measures which the government is favouring will eliminate a scarcity of goods which is partly the cause of inflation and the desire on the part of many people to purchase them.


It also discourages the building of houses. An increasing number of Canadians desire to own homes but as was admitted today in the house there is a decreased number of housing units being built. It is also likely to make these units more expensive.
As I mentioned before, by the expansion of money the productive industry of this country is going to be discouraged, which will result in further scarcities. I note that the president of the Canadian gas association has stated that gas distribution is likely to be seriously threatened, which in turn will affect the sale of gas-burning equipment. Consequently the householders in every city where gas may be distributed will be affected. On the other hand, luxury items enjoy a bigger spread or margin of profit, and those industries are not likely to be as seriously affected as are the industries supplying necessary goods. But curtailment of credit affects every Canadian industry adversely.
There is another rather alarming angle to this, Mr. Speaker, and it is that the credit curbs do not affect United States investors. They can bring their money over here and invest it. That is exactly what is happening; and the thing we wanted to get away from, more and more control by Americans of our raw resources, is going to be magnified and increased rather than decreased by the action of the government in its attempt to control inflation. In my opinion the controls are just ten years too late. If the government had thought about this when it was mentioned years ago instead of now when the dollar is only worth a few cents they would have been doing something.
It is of interest to note when I am talking about interest rates that I had as a visitor at my home just a week ago an agricultural expert from Switzerland. I asked him about the value of farm property there, and he told me the average would be $1,000 per acre. I asked him about the price of milk and other products produced there and I said, "How in the world do you ever pay off the mortgage if you buy a 60-acre farm for $60,000?" He said, "Why, the people in Switzerland who have money do not want us to pay off the mortgages. They will lend us money at approximately 21 per cent and they are glad to have these mortgages go on for generations as long as they are sure of their 2J per cent." I am not certain what rate is being charged today by the Canadian

farm loan board but I imagine it is around 5 per cent, or double the rate at which the Swiss people are able to borrow money in the form of farm loans.
I would also point out that Switzerland has money for export. The people of Switzerland are not going to the United States for money to develop their country. Yet although Canada has vast resources, people from the United States are able to come here and invest their money because we are so poor from paying taxes. Thirty-one cents out of every dollar that we take in goes out in taxes to our government. No wonder we have not money to invest in our natural resources.
It is also a bit alarming to read that some 500 bankruptcies occurred during the past year, or almost up to the level of the depression years. Curtailment of credit will not bring about an increase in goods, and therefore I doubt whether it will be very effective in controlling inflation.
It has not been my practice in the past to say anything about international affairs because there were others who were making detailed studies of the problems, but the developments during the last few months have struck home into the hearts of every Canadian, and I think what I have to say reflects the thinking of the vast majority of my constituents. The resignation yesterday of Prime Minister Eden came as a shock to most of us, but it only served to bring into focus the tremendous burden under which the leader of the United Kingdom government has been labouring for many months.
We should not forget that when Eden and Mollet were endeavouring to prevent a communist coup in the Middle East, brought about by the ineffectiveness of the United Nations, the Canadian government played a role that tormented France and Britain and gave solace to our enemies. Last night's news only served to emphasize that statement. The United States, in the midst of a presidential campaign, chose to be against Britain and France; but now we see the president and congress trying desperately to regain lost ground. Resolutions of the United Nations condemning Britain and France were adopted, but I think more and more people will come to the conclusion that the only mistake Eden made was that he left the Middle East too soon. Britain and France left in the hope that their retirement would help the cause of world peace and would preserve the United Nations.
The Address-Mr. H. O. White
Have Russia or Hungary respected the pious resolutions of the United Nations? While untold thousands suffered the United Nations dared not even send an observer to Hungary. It is rather interesting to note that Mr. Nehru has been shocked by the events in Hungary. I would suggest it has taken him a long time to realize what most of us in the western world have known since the close of world war I.
It has been my privilege to meet some of the Hungarian refugees and to hear something of their desperate fight for freedom at first hand. But what did the United Nations do? Nothing but talk. Hungary has revealed to the world that the will to be free is strong in the face of terrible odds. Hungary has revealed the communist world in its true light, ruthless and out for world conquest. Hungary has revealed the United Nations as an idealistic but impotent force. The United Nations must face realities or perish.
I turn to another phase of Canada's role in international affairs, that of foreign aid. In the past I have supported enthusiastically the Colombo plan and other plans devised to assist the so-called have-not or backward nations. But when the Suez crisis arose some of these so-called have-not nations were able to put into action a more efficient navy and air force than Canada is able to summon after spending nearly $2 billion a year since Korea. This makes me wonder whether we can bribe these foreign countries or buy their loyalty. I am afraid that all that is happening is that they are damning us because we do not give them more. At the very time we were able to supply this foreign aid the maritimes asked for financial backing for their bonds to build hydroelectric and other projects, and they were even refused the backing of the federal government. In western Canada there are many developments that could have been undertaken but they were held in abeyance, probably for the next election.
As far as I personally am concerned, events in the past few months have but served to sour the milk of human kindness. The government and all Canadians should work to strengthen the ties of the commonwealth, because after all the commonwealth of nations is probably the single greatest factor for peace in the world. I think the role of the commonwealth should be as a balance of power between the United States on the one hand and the U.S.S.R. on the other. As such it can probably maintain the peace of the world, but only if we have a strong, united commonwealth.
Trade policies and all other measures that can be devised should be aimed at

The Address-Mr. Philpott bringing the commonwealth together. Finally I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs by way of paraphrase of psalm 144, "Lead us not into captivity."

Mr. Speaker, first may I add my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I refer not only to such members as the hon. member for Gloucester but the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr, Michaud) and other Acadian members.
While I am still in the congratulatory mood, and before I get around to the strike, may I also congratulate my old friend the new Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) on the skilful way in which he spoke yesterday for nearly two hours, I think, and said absolutely nothing.

I thought he did a much better job the night before on television. I thought we perhaps have a new television star arising in Canada. I think the new Leader of the Opposition was better when he was explaining his own omissions or errors or whatever you call them that the newspapermen were putting up to him than he was yesterday when he was setting out to criticize the government. It seemed to me that he did not say yes and he did not say no. He was waiting to see whether the government was going to do something, in which case he would have said they should have done nothing; or he was waiting to see whether the government was going to do nothing, in which case he would have said that they should have done something.
Before I talk about the strike I may say that I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is waiting for some extremely good

news later on in the day. As far as I am concerned, I am quite willing to sit down at any time when he has that announcement which we are all waiting to hear and about the coming of which the hon. member who spoke immediately preceding me did not seem to be so pleased.
I do not want to keep the house too long on this matter, but I for one believe that we are now successfully coming to the end of one of the most potentially dangerous situations that we have ever had in Canada. I for one believe that this extremely difficult situation we have had in the past couple of weeks in Canada has been admirably handled by the present government. It seems to me that there were two clear-cut issues involved in this work stoppage. The first issue involved that certainly directly concerns us here as members of parliament, lawmakers for this great Dominion of Canada, was this: Should a democratic parliament in a democratic country forbid such a strike? If so, should it do so under all conditions or just under some conditions?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it would be a terrible mistake for Canada or any other democratic country that prides itself on freedom of action to put an arbitrary ban on the right to strike of any great group of Canadian workers, whether those workers happen to be railway workers or others. I am quite well aware of the fact that in a utility such as the great railroads where actual life and death, and the prosperity of so many of the people, depend on the continued service of the railway, no government-neither this government or any other one-could long permit an interruption in the service of so vital a utility. But in a true democracy I submit that you must always balance the things on both sides.
I know that in any police state, whether it is a fascist police state or a communist police state, the first act of any dictatorial government in regard to the industrial set-up of the country is to forbid the holding of strikes. I believe that any democracy-and this applies to Canada or any other democracy-takes an extremely unwise step when it arbitrarily passes an over-all law forbidding a strike. But in any event, surely the proof of the pudding is in the eating. I think the diplomatic, wise and fair way in which the government of Canada has handled this present work stoppage in Canada, as to which we all hope at any time to hear of an amicable settlement having been arrived at acceptable to all concerned, is surely the preferable way.
We all know that the basis on which this work stoppage is going to be settled, when

it is settled, is this. It will be settled on the basis that work will be resumed more or less on the basis of the status quo. There will be certain adjustments of wages and so on. There has been no great insoluble problem in that regard. The main problem which has not been settled will be left to further consideration under some kind of a fair test by some sort of tribunal which will carry more weight with the Canadian people.
I cannot share the suggestions made earlier this afternoon by my friend the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) in two respects. I certainly cannot share with him the suggestion that the government of Canada should go to the arbitrary length of putting in a controller to run the Canadian Pacific Railway. The C.P.R. is an institution of which every Canadian citizen should be proud. There is nothing in our whole national life that has contributed more to the welfare and prosperity of this great Canadian nation than has the great Canadian Pacific Railway. We ought to be proud of the management. If the management has some kind of suggestion which it thinks will improve the operation of the railway, of course every sensible person will listen to that suggestion.
In the second place, I do not agree with the hon. member for Regina City when he says that no lawyer should be allowed to sit on the board. I was a little bit puzzled by his speech, because he spent exactly half his time lauding the findings of one lawyer who happens to be on the board-perhaps because he is a Liberal lawyer-and denouncing all other lawyers and saying that no lawyer should be allowed to sit on the board.
