speechtext:
I have no objection to lawyers, so long as we do not get too many of them at the same time. It seems to me that there were two things wrong with the conciliation hearing which was held. The first thing that was wrong was quite simple; there was not enough publicity. I am a member of this House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, and I try to do my job, as I think most of the other members of this house do. I, for one, confess that I know practically nothing about the findings of the board of conciliation except what I have read in the newspapers since this strike started. I think we have to have a tribunal of the kind that will focus the whole publicity of this country on what is involved in this issue, because the most binding law in any democracy, including Canada, is the law of common sense.
What is involved in this work stoppage is this. Is it or is it not safe to operate diesel
The Address-Mr. Philpott engine locomotives with a one-man crew?
I submit that contrary to what a good many people seem to assume, the only conclusion reached by two of the three members of the conciliation board was what I would call the old Scottish verdict of not proven. Certainly they did not settle the argument, and in my opinion the argument cannot be settled. As a layman who has travelled quite often over the railway lines of both systems to the far west coast, I am very much in the position of the man from Missouri when it comes to saying that a one-man crew can ever safely operate any kind of engine down through the Fraser valley, whether it is on a passenger train or a freight train. I have been on those trains when it has taken a whole 24 hours to go from the peak of the Rocky mountains down to the coast, and when they required all their crew up in the front end to be on the lookout for the hazards of the day.
I say, therefore, nobody should assume that because this tribunal is going to be set up to focus the attention of all the people of Canada on this great question, is it or is it not safe to operate diesel locomotives with one-man crews, that the finding is automatically going to be that it is safe at all times and in all circumstances.
I have here a brief submitted, certainly to myself and I assume to other members of parliament, by local 657 of the brotherhood of locomotive engineers. I would submit that the locomotive engineers of Canada are a most responsible body of men in whose hands we literally entrust our lives day after day, week after week, all year round. Here are some of the things they say on page 2 of this brief:
It would not be possible or practicable to list here all the incidents in which the fireman helper has established his worth, the saving of human lives and valuable property. However for the purpose of this review the following is set forth: When trainman Martin on August 22nd, 1955, got off the engine at Glacier, B.C. in order to make a running inspection of his train he slipped and his body contacted the spring rigging of the lead Diesel unit he continued to turn over and over in a rolling fashion, but unable to get away from the side of the locomotive. Fireman helper, Saari, was at his station, and because of his instantaneous action the train was brought to an immediate stop. Trainman Martin suffered among other injuries a broken back. However he has now recovered and has resumed his normal occupation, but he freely states that but for the fact that the fireman helper (engineer's eyes) it would be impossible for him to be alive today.
On September 30, 1950, a locomotive was being turned on the Wye at Glacier, B.C. In the absence of a trainman the fireman was throwing switches: a child playing on the left side of the engine which had passed out of the view of both the engineer and the fireman was struck down and died 24 hours later. It was without question established at the coroner's inquest that if the fireman had been at his station in the cab of the engine, this tragic death could not have occurred.

The Address-Mr. Philpott
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit when this tribunal sits, as it will sit to settle this question of whether one-man operation is safe as well as efficient for the country, the men who actually operate the trains, whether they are passenger trains or freight trains, will have to have their say and they will have to have their say in a forum which will enable the people of Canada to hear what they are saying. When the tribunal makes its findings, in my opinion all of the people of Canada, who are 99 and 44-100th's per cent law-abiding, will loyally accept the findings.
There is one point I should like to make here, and it is this. There is no greater fallacy than the idea that the trade unionists are automatically opposed to automation. There is no class in our whole industrial society in North America so well aware of the value of the machine in raising wages as the skilled mechanics who operate those machines. Every skilled mechanic who operates any kind of great machine knows that the more expensive the machine he is operating, in 99 cases out of 100, the higher are his wages because the more skilled person he has to be to operate that machine. As Walter Reuther and other great trade union leaders have pointed out in recent months, labour is not opposed to automation; trade unions are not opposed to automation. All the trade unionist demands is that there should be a fair transition from the old methods to the new.
No, Mr. Speaker; labour knows very well that the machine is the best friend of the man who operates the machine, and that the more machines you have in the country the more of the products of the machines you have to divide amongst your population. The difference between a very poor and backward country and a very rich and advanced country, like Canada or the United States, is that we have the machine as our servant and other people do not.
I wish to turn now, Mr. Speaker, very briefly to one other topic. We are going to have an election this year. Contrary to what some of my friends opposite might expect, I make no prediction. I think that is presumption on the part of anyone who really attempts to believe in democracy. I say to my hon. friends whom I see smiling over at me that I hope they do better this year.
I am all for them. I believe in the two-party system. I think that alternatives to the present government are always necessary if our democracy is to have real vitality. I rejoice in the fact that the great Conservative party has found a fit and worthy successor to that great Canadian who sat for several


years in the position of leader of the opposition. I refer, of course to my old friend George Drew.
In my opinion the election of 1957 is going to hinge very largely on one important point, and that is which party which is or aspires to be the government of Canada can contribute most to the paramount question in the world today, the question of war and peace. I submit that there is no more practical team of peacemakers in the world today than the team represented by that great and distinguished Canadian the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) and his associate in the field of foreign affairs, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I submit that on their own record they are the most practical pair of peacemakers in the world today.
As I see it, the foreign policy of Canada, the peacemaking policy of Canada, is based on four solid cornerstones. The first solid cornerstone of the Canadian peacemaking policy is Canadian nationality, pride in Canada as a dominion-yes, I am proud of that term "dominion"-but as a nation, too. Only this week some of us here witnessed the ceremony of the unveiling of that fine statue to that great Canadian and Conservative, Sir Robert Borden. I listened, I think it was last night or perhaps it was the night before, over the radio to someone interviewing the very distinguished woman sculptor who did that fine statue of Sir Robert Borden. The young man who was interviewing this great artist of whom every Canadian should be proud asked this distinguished Toronto lady what it was she looked for in Sir Robert Borden to try to put in that bronze and on that stone. She said this: "When I read and reread the life of Sir Robert Borden I found that he was a great Canadian nationalist". She said, "I got his Canadian nationhood standing foursquare in the way that he has his two feet planted on the ground". The only place I ever differ with my hon. friend's opposite in the official opposition is when they sometimes think there is some conflict between a robust Canadian nationalism and a 100 per cent loyalty to that great organization that we call the British commonwealth.
I submit that the second cornerstone in the peacemaking policy of the present government is the undying loyalty to and fervent faith in the great organization which we call the British commonwealth. No government that now exists or has ever existed on earth has done more to maintain and strengthen that great organization than this present Liberal government of Canada that sits here today. If I had to choose between all the

international organizations that exist, between NATO and the United Nations and the British commonwealth, and I could have my say so we could keep only one of those international organizations, without a minute's hesitation I would say, "I will stand by the British commonwealth" because the British commonwealth is an organic thing that has grown up on the basis of the actual trials and tribulations of history over the centuries. We must keep the British commonwealth and keep it alive and vital. Where I sometimes differ from some of my hon. friends is that the British commonwealth they have in mind is a purely imaginary thing. We are dealing with a British commonwealth that actually exists.
We had a crisis not so many weeks ago over Suez. In my opinion it was an entirely unnecessary crisis; for every good thing that that great statesman, Sir Anthony Eden, tried to do in the wrong way by his ill advice, perhaps stupidly, without consultation, he could have done more effectively in the right way, keeping the 100 per cent support of the British commonwealth and of all the loyal members of the United Nations. I submit that on that occasion we had the third and fourth cornerstones of the peacemaking policy of the present Liberal government of Canada very well exemplified, because Canada stepped into the breach to restore and bridge again the gap that had been developed between the great allies of this western alliance. Canada stepped in to repair the damage that had been done to the United Nations. If that was disloyalty to the British commonwealth, as I have heard some people suggest, it is a very strange kind of disloyalty indeed.
When I was reading of the very great and historic events that have taken place in and around the holy land, Egypt and the Suez canal in the past few weeks, and especially when I got to thinking that the actual war itself had started in the Sinai peninsula, the very spot where Moses, the great lawgiver himself, brought down the ten commandments that became the basis of all civilized law wherever civilized men are, I went back to the original source and read the fascinating story. I read all about Gaza. We have been reading about Gaza and the Gaza strip in the last few weeks, and so on. One of the principal
reasons he did not come to Alberta was that he did not believe in taking social credit into political life. Because Premier Aber-hart did believe in that there was created a certain amount of unhappiness between Major Douglas and Premier Aberhart. I would imagine that is just about the most satisfactory explanation. They were both powerful men, they were both dynamic gentlemen, great in every respect. I knew them both; I think that is the explanation. I think almost any person who has had any experience will realize that.
I should have said that the quotation I have read is from page 97 of the evidence taken before the agricultural committee of the Alberta legislature, published in 1934. On that same page 97 he was asked, "What is Social Credit?" and he said:
Social Credit from the technical point of view is simply the power to monetize real wealth. That is very nearly a complete definition of social financial credit. The power to monetize real wealth is now a monopoly. We want the power to monetize and distribute money to be public property.
It could not be better put although he was speaking extemporaneously at the time. He gave that comprehensive definition of Social Credit. What is the meaning of the expression "monetizing real wealth" as it is used in that quotation? To monetize real wealth means to turn real wealth into money. Ordinarily we think that the only way in which we can turn real wealth such as goods into money is to sell the goods. That is the first thing that orthodox people think about it, but there is another means which Major Douglas had in mind. I should like to give a few examples of this matter of turning real wealth into money.
First there is the ordinary I.O.U. with which every hon. member of the house is familiar. For instance, a man may say, "I.O.U. one ton of coal" or "I.O.U. one hour's work" or "I.O.U. five pounds of sugar." Such an I.O.U. could be passed from one man to another in payment for many things and would probably affect four or five persons before it came back to be honoured by the person who wrote it out. Such an I.O.U. would be a ticket to claim goods or services. Any ticket to claim goods or services is a form of monetizing those goods and services.


It could be passed from one person to another as a medium of exchange, which is the first definition of money.
Then it is a store of value. As long as it stands for five pounds of sugar or one ton of coal it is a store of value. A unit of money such as a one dollar bill is merely a medium of exchange and a ticket to goods. Therefore an I.O.U. made by a man owning a ton of coal or five pounds of sugar is in effect the monetizing of that coal or sugar which he has, and it would be something that could be used as money if people accepted it as such.
Speaking broadly, any person or group of persons who creates or brings into existence any claim to goods or services or any instrument which could be employed as a unit of money is monetizing those goods and services, providing the people concerned are willing to accept that instrument as money. That of course is the all-important point, that the people readily accept it as money.
What are some other examples of units of money in Canadian history created by the monetizing of goods and services? A good many people think Social Credit is something new. It has been in existence almost ever since human beings have been on this earth. May I list a few such examples as they are described in a booklet entitled, "The Story of Canada's Currency", published for the Bank of Canada in 1955. One famous kind of early Canadian currency was Hudson's Bay tokens. From page 8 of the booklet I read:
Hudson's Bay tokens. These Hudson's Bay Company tokens represented the unit of currency used in the fur trade for many decades. The largest, one "made-beaver", was equal in value to the skin of an adult male beaver in prime condition. Smaller sizes represented one-half, one-quarter and one-eighth "made-beaver". Before these brass tokens came into use, a made-beaver was represented by a stick, a porcupine quill, an ivory disc, a musket ball or anything else agreed upon by trader and trapper. The trapper would be handed a number of the units agreed upon representing the value of his catch and with these would make his purchases from the store. The tokens were designed by George Simpson MeTavish of Albany Fort in 1854.
What the Hudson's Bay Company had done there when it made these tokens was to create in effect an I.O.U. which was backed by all the goods the company had in its stores or which the company would have in its stores right up to the time the person who had received the tokens came and recovered the goods. In other words they monetized those goods.
Another famous kind of Canadian currency was playing card money, first issued in 1685

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
by the French colonial authorities. From page 7 of the booklet I read:
Although card money began as a short term financial device it was not long before the cards began to circulate among people as a medium of common exchange and later issues of card money were provided with this specific aim in mind. With the passage of time card money became an important part of the currency of French Canada and remained until the fall of Quebec in 1759.
In this case it is not so easy to see that the money created was a monetization of any particular bit of wealth, as was the case with the Hudson's Bay tokens which monetized all the goods in the Hudson's Bay stores. In the case of the French Canadian card money an attempt was made to monetize all the goods and services being produced in the area which was using the card money, because the card money would be a demand or claim on any goods or services in that area. The claim was made good because people accepted the cards as money.
From 1800 to 1855 they began using another kind of money. May I read from page 14 of this same little pamphlet to which I have already referred:
The demand for currency in these times also stimulated the practice of merchants issuing "bons" good for the face value in merchandise. From 1800 to 1837 a very large part of the small change in circulation consisted of these merchants' tokens.
When the merchant issued one of these tokens he simply monetized the goods which were in his store and would be in his store until such time as the token was brought back to the store to be redeemed in goods. I go on:
Many were copper penny and half penny tokens of good quality imported from Britain but these were gradually replaced by lighter tokens of copper or brass.
Then further down:
In the latter period these sometimes took the form of store cards bearing the merchant's name, address and frequently the type of business.
There you have once more tokens, monetizations of goods, instruments of money, instruments of credit created by people with the goods to sell. In the particular town where I grew up there were two stores when I was a small boy, one called H. S. Allen and Company and the other called the Cardston Co-Operative Mercantile Institution. Each of these issued little tokens which they called scrip. We used scrip. I can remember seeing my mother come in with butter and eggs and various other produce, turn them in to the store, receive scrip for the goods, and go out and buy the things she needed to buy with this scrip. It was good. There was no need of having gold behind it. There was no need of having the Bank of Canada behind
it or the Dominion of Canada behind it. The scrip was accepted almost readily as cash.

Then the money can be made of paper or, as was the case with the Hudson's Bay Company, even porcupine quills.
I propose to leave other things I could say concerning the Canadian financial system and come down to the finance act. Those who have read the financial history of Canada remember that in 1868 there was passed what was called the Dominion Notes Act. The Dominion Notes Act empowered the government of Canada to create tickets, "made-beavers", if you like, "playing card money", if you like, dollars that would be acceptable from coast to coast in Canada. When we come down to 1914 we find that there was passed, as a measure in connection with the

The Address-Mr. Blackmore war, the finance act of 1914, later re-enacted by the Liberals as the finance act of 1923.
Here are some of the things that were done under the finance act of 1914. They issued $26 million of bills backed by railway securities and spent them into circulation as part of the national revenue. They created $10 million in bills backed by nothing in particular except the credit of Canada, namely the ability of Canada in that case to deliver goods and services. They created $50 million in 1917 and bought horses, harness, grain and other supplies that were needed in conducting the war and sent those goods over to Britain. Britain used them to fight the war. Those $50 million were good money. The farmers who received them had no objection. They were just as good as any other money. They had nothing behind them except that they were a claim on goods in Canada.
What could be done under the finance act of 1914 one would certainly think would be possible to be done in Canada today. If it is not possible today in Canada to do what was done in 1914, then whoever thinks it is not, had better prepare himself to stand before this house and justify his position with great care.
Social Credit need not hesitate for a minute to talk about creating money. It has been done all through Canadian history.
One of the important things concerning this 1914 act and what was done under it was this. Much of the money was spent into circulation. That $50 million, that $26 million and that $10 million could have been used to pay old age pensions. It could have been used in bringing down the price of goods by a discount. It was spent into circulation.
We went on under the finance act reenacted in 1923 by a Liberal government. Just at this point may I recall that it was a Conservative government that enacted the finance act of 1914, and that it was a Liberal government which had seen the act in operation all during world war I, which re-enacted it as the finance act of 1923, notwithstanding the fact that they might have been suspected of having political animosity toward the legislation because they did not introduce it. If that is not clear proof that our forefathers of 1914 and 1923 saw the possibilities of the government creating money and spending it into circulation, backed only by goods and services and the producing capacity of the country, then where would you go to find evidence that would prove anything?
What is the limit of creating and circulating such money? The general limit of it must be the amount of goods there are in the


country. Since money, after all, is a ticket to goods, a claim to goods, it would be dangerous and unsocial to create more money than there were goods. On the other hand, if it is desired to be able to create more money and have it in the country, the first thing we must look after is the production of more goods. If the Minister of Finance at the present time were budgeting on a basis of that sort and were wondering where he was going to get the money to pay twice as big old age pensions, the first thing he would do would be to look into the matter of increasing Canada's production by an amount large enough to justify the creation of the necessary money. Thus he would have in his hands a means whereby he could bring about any kind of condition of prosperity within the country by the simple device of increasing production.

Let us now take the Bank of Canada, which was set up in 1934 under the act passed in that year, and see what has been done under the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada, when it was set up, had the power to create money almost limitlessly. The one thing that stood in the way was that a certain amount of gold was required. But as the result of amendments to the act which were made in 1940, I am told, the Bank of Canada no longer is obliged to have gold as a backing for money. The Bank of Canada can take a $1 million dominion bond, turn it into money

and let the government have that $1 million and spend it as part of the national revenue if there are enough goods to spend it on; and there will be no cost except for the little bit of paper, ink and so on involved. This is extremely important. What Social Crediters say is this. Since we have this Bank of Canada with all the power which the finance act had, in the name of common sense, and in the interests of Canada why not use it not only to lend to people money with which to produce, but let people have it with which to buy up to the point where they buy either what they need, or all there is to buy. That is the Social Credit position. It is simple.
Having indicated what is the centre, the pivot, the heart or the core of the Social Credit idea, namely the creation of money to represent goods, may I now turn to the financial technique of Social Credit? When money is created the first thing that is done with it is to bring down the price of goods to the consumer. If you are worried about the rise in prices, why not use the compensated discount to bring down the price of goods? Why not? The result would be exemplified by this: If it be found that a pair of shoes is being sold at $10 and we want to bring the price down to $9, why not give to the merchant instructions that he may sell that pair of shoes for $9, turn in the bill to the bank and be compensated with $1 and given credit for $10? Then the bank will turn in the bill to the Receiver General of Canada and receive the $1. In this way, by the simple use of this government power to create money, the price of shoes would be brought down 10 per cent.
The same kind of principle could be applied to all the goods in Canada, bringing down the price of those goods. We are not obliged to be absolutely slaves to these conditions which are arising around us and causing so much difficulty. Would that course not be far better sense than to let the Bank of Canada raise the discount rate and force up the interest to people who are producing, thereby forcing up the cost of production and forcing up the cost of goods, and then hypocritically call that inflation?
Now, the hon. member for Peace River reminds me that it would be optional for the merchant to do that sort of thing, but Social Credit is based on the principle of cooperation. Surely people have sense enough to co-operate when they see something is to their advantage. If they do not, let them wait for a while until they have lost their trade through the competition of others who are co-operating.
The third principle of Social Credit is this. If the amount of money which is in circulation in the country as a result of the compensated discount and as a result of the
The Address-Mr. Blackmore money which is lent out for production in the form of farm loans and the like is not enough to enable the people of Canada as a whole to buy the production of Canada up to the desirable point, then issue the people dividends of created money, personal issues of purchasing power, which will enable them to buy up to the point at which consumption in Canada will equate the production in Canada.
The people will naturally ask, has this Social Credit ever been tried? I say, not under that name. For some most interesting reason the people who have money, and certain great forces that are seeking to enslave the world, are fighting Social Credit with a vigour that the fiends from the infernal pit would envy. They have such control over the press and the other means of teaching people that they delude people and keep them from accepting Social Credit and entering into a state of prosperity and security which is right here if we only had the wisdom to adopt the measures to make it available to the people of Canada.

speechtext: That would be impossible, unless the Conservatives could come and join us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At least then we might see some sharp differences in policies and platforms.
However, it is a privilege, Mr. Speaker, to have this opportunity to speak in the debate on the reply to the speech from the throne, it is a privilege and a duty, a duty I think to say something of what the people are feeling and thinking in one's own particular constituency and area, to do your best to try to put across what they feel to be the important political and governmental considerations. I think this debate, more than any other, gives us an opportunity to do just that. Before I commence on that I want to take the opportunity of sincerely congratulating the


mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robi-chaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They come from widely separated parts of the country and exhibited a sense of urgency in their well-prepared addresses in regard to the problems with which they are faced. They showed also a degree of aggressiveness and optimism, particularly in the case of the hon. member for Gloucester, that was very refreshing in this house. Altogether they embodied a spirit of cohesion and unity that I hope will always remain the same in so far as our great party is concerned.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, traditionally one should say something about one's own constituency. I want to do this in relation to two matters in particular, because I cannot cover the whole gamut of the measures that are proposed in the throne speech. First of all I want to discuss Canadian foreign policy, because I think that now the Middle East situation has more or less found a temporary calmness, it is a good time to bring to bear the thoughts one has in that regard. Second, I want to talk about something that is entirely unrelated, and that is the question of taxation for education on the municipal level. I chose these two subjects because I think it is about those two matters that people are feeling most strongly in the metropolitan area with which I am acquainted.
First of all I just want to take a moment to acquaint you with two or three physical facts about the constituency I represent. Hon. members will be glad to know that the Scarborough bluffs are still standing. I received a copy of the preliminary population totals for the Dominion of Canada showing changes in population in the municipalities in Canada that are most interesting.
I noted that in the municipality of Scarborough we had an increase from 56,000 to 139,000 in the years 1951 to 1956. That is an increase of 83,000 people. In the municipality of North York, a great part of which is included in the constituency of York-Scarborough, we had an increase in population in those years from 85,000 to 168,000, again, oddly enough, an increase of 83,000 people. That gives the house an idea of the tremendous growth that is taking place in the population. If you look through the list of municipalities across the country, with the exception of the township of Etobicoke in the metropolitan area of Toronto I do not think you will find any place with anywhere near a similar increase in population. Hon. members can understand the problems that arise when such a condition occurs, and not necessarily just political problems, in trying to meet and know the 83,000 new people.

We are very prolific in this area, but I imagine that apart from the natural growth a great number of the people moved into the area from outside. The problems arising from this growth are very difficult to handle. From the federal point of view we have the usual one of postal service. It has taken a great deal of one's time to cope with the situation in so far as the delivery of mail is concerned, which is a most important function of the federal government. We have had an increase of 30,000 in actual points of call on door to door delivery in my constituency alone. We have just finished constructing a new post office in Scarborough, and no sooner had we opened it than it was filled to capacity. It will shortly require an extension, making it twice the size it is now. I have urged the Post Office Department to undertake a survey in another great part of the constituency which is growing rapidly. This survey is to commence very shortly. I would encourage the Post Office Department to develop a sense of urgency about the need for this postal service.
It is not always easy for the civil service here in Ottawa to visualize the extent of this growth that is taking place. It is not easy for people who have a particular job to do, and who are busy doing that particular job, to make themselves go out and initiate proceedings and surveys that in the final analysis are going to mean more work and more problems for themselves. I do find that the post office department in Toronto need a great deal of encouragement to initiate activity that will provide the increase in services that we so greatly need.
Problems of transportation also arise. We have, I think, about 56 level crossings in the township of Scarborough alone, at one of which there was a recent fatality. We know that it is well nigh impossible to get the money to provide underpasses and do away with level crossings. I think the report we received last year stated that it would cost $600 million merely to convert 10 per cent of the existing grade crossings. Obviously this points to a need for more thinking on the part of those responsible for proper protection devices at the existing grade crossings. We have also been urging that this be done.
On the economic side, employment is satisfactory in my constituency. There have been some soft spots in certain businesses such as the building trades. I do not want to deal at length with the situation in house construction at this time, though I would like to speak on it later in the session, but it is a fact that the so-called tight money policy of the government has created quite a change 82715-74
The Address-Mr. Enfield in the building industry in those fast-growing areas. You have all read recently of the demise, or should I say bankruptcy, of the largest real estate trading firm in the dominion. I think that was a situation where,, because of over extension of credit facilities, or over extension of the use of credit, the firm found itself in close juxtaposition with this tight money policy and could not obtain that credit. This will result in the slowing down of the development of great areas of land where normally a great deal of house building would take place.
I am not saying that this is right or wrongv I am saying, however, that monetary policy, and the method we are using in dealing with it, represents a fairly new science, and t would urge the government to keep a careful eye on its means of measuring the impact of the policy it has instituted so it can decide just when to draw the line and encourage the opposite effect to take place. I think that is the theory, to use what monetary means you have at your disposal to try to iron out the peaks and valleys; but the problem is, when do you make your move? I have great confidence that the government will not let the tight money policy go so far as to cause a decrease particularly in house building, which I think is the basis of our economy, to the point where it is going to create a hardship on anyone.
I have digressed a little from my original plan, and I want to go back and talk briefly on the question of Canada's foreign policy, with particular reference to the Middle East situation. In this debate on the speech from the throne many members have mentioned this subject. In the past three years that has not always been done. In fact in the past I have never felt competent to discuss it at all.
I think we all suffer in various degrees from a lack of personal knowledge of and personal experience with the facts that govern foreign policy, which prevents us from feeling overly confident to discuss the subject; therefore I wish to state my view very briefly.
It is this. In this last crisis there was a great divergence of opinion among the people in my constituency as to the action taken by the United Kingdom. There was a sharp cleavage, in fact. The interesting thing about it was that people were either all for the move on the one hand or all against it on the other, with very few taking a sort of neutral watching ground in between. This resulted in widespread confusion on the subject and the result of the action that was taken in the Middle East. It was followed by a depressed attitude owing to the cleavage between the emotions perhaps, on the one hand, where the feeling



The Address-Mr. Enfield was to back the move, and on the other the reasoning which suggested that we had suffered an obvious loss of prestige and power in the Middle East that resulted from the sequence of events.
It was from this position that the people looked to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for their leadership in this crisis. I know I can report very accurately that public opinion in my constituency, and I think everywhere in Canada, is enthusiastic in its acclaim of the stand taken by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this crisis, and is unanimous in the feeling that as a result Canada has gained in stature in world leadership. But to be fair we must emphasize that people were shocked and indeed appalled at the rapid transposition that took place from a solid group forming the western alliance to a position in the United Nations wherein overnight great stresses and strains developed and we found the United States taking a stand directly opposite to the stand taken by Great Britain. I think it showed to many people that the United Nations has a long way to go. I believe it revealed great weaknesses in the United Nation's organization, and I am convinced that people still have a feeling of insecurity and uncertainty as a nesult. We in Canada have given our support unstintingly to the United Nations. In some respects we have had the ground knocked out from under our feet by the events that have taken place; and we must not forget this, because it means we have to urge our leaders in the United Nations, our Canadian representatives, to do everything possible to strengthen this organization, to suggest policies and forms of activity that will make it a stronger working group so that with a feeling of security and conviction we can back a group which we know is going to be an effective international body.
After all, the whole principle on which our foreign policy is based is one of containment of the Russian power and its satellites, a policy of containment based on the philosophy that things do not always remain the same, that with the passage of time there will be a softening of the attitude of those we call the enemy and a modus operandi arrived at whereby the two groups, or perhaps three groups in our world, will find themselves able to work completely together and there will be lasting peace. That type of philosophy depends entirely on building up a solid western alliance and a true United Nations group.
We would like, then, in our constituency the following questions to be answered in regard to foreign policy. To what extent can Canada make its own independent influence

felt in the United Nations? Must the question always be "As the United States goes so goes the United Nations"? What is the meaning of the unilateral action taken by the United States in recent days in the Middle East? What is happening to NATO? Will the combination of the current economic crisis in Britain and the reduction of French and British forces in Europe drastically alter the course of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization? These are questions that I myself, and I think my constituents, would like to see answered, and if there are no positive answers we would like to see these questions thoroughly explored.
I would like now, Mr. Speaker, to turn to the other portion of my submission in this debate, which is entirely unrelated to what has gone before. As I said previously, this portion of my address concerns the field of taxation with regard to education in the metropolitan area. There was reference in the throne speech to an increase in grants for certain types of education, and this is something I believe everyone was pleased to see. From time to time there is a wide and insistent expression of opinion from provincial and municipal authorities that the federal government should do something in order to aid education. I find these expressions of opinion are not always accompanied by information that would make it possible to give every consideration to the request.
For example, I received a letter some time ago from the board of control of the city of Toronto requesting that the city be given greater aid through the taxation of federally-owned properties in the city. There was nothing in that letter to indicate what the impact would be of such aid, what it would mean in terms of increasing tax revenues. I found on reading the Globe and Mail yesterday morning that the city may gain about $800,000 under this measure that is mentioned in the throne speech.
I think the fundamental question here is this. If these bodies are going to ask for further financial aid from the federal government in a field that is historically and legally that of the province and municipality, then we are put in a position where we have to examine the entire financial structure of the province and municipality themselves. We cannot simply say, "Well, fine, you need aid, and we will give you aid". We have a responsibility for these trust moneys that we call taxes to the people from whom we collect them. We have only a certain legal basis on which we can expend them; therefore we must look into the method the provinces employ in collecting and expending taxes, or receive full information from the provinces

as to just why they find themselves unable to carry out what has always been their job, a job of which they are very jealous in many parts of the country.
Despite this, when it is said, "Why do we not do something to aid education," the fact that we are aiding education considerably seems to be completely ignored. In the 1955-56 session of parliament I put a question on the order paper. I want to read it now because I received an extremely full answer, and I think it is very revealing. The question appears at page 3728 of Hansard for May 9, 1956, and reads as follows:
During the fiscal year 1955-56, what sums of money by way of outright grants, bursaries, scholarships and loans were expended by the federal government directly in aid of education in Canada, including grants for assistance to Indians and Eskimos; (a) by each department of government in each province, for aid to university students, and including professional training; (b) by each department of government in each province for education cn the secondary and elementary school levels?
I tried to cover all aspects of education in the question because on going through the estimates I found that grants, scholarships, bursaries and loans were scattered all the way through the different departments of government for various courses and aspects of education. I cannot possibly put on the record all the details of the information that is contained in the answer. The total aid to education provided by the government in the year 1955-56 amounted to over $28 million. I should like to place on record what has been spent in the various provinces, because it may be of some value to hon. members. The expenditures to the nearest thousand dollars were as follows:
British Columbia	 $2,989,000
Alberta	 2,261,000
Saskatchewan	 1,862,000
Manitoba	 1,437,000
Ontario	 7,228,000
Quebec	 2,952,000
New Brunswick	 739,000
Nova Scotia	 1,007,000
Prince Edward Island	 123,000
Newfoundland	 422,000
Yukon	 76,000
Northwest Territories	 1,025,000
It will be seen that we are expending considerable amounts in our efforts to aid education. It is not true to say that we are doing nothing in this field. These expenditures are spread out through the departments because these totals are made up of a tremendous number of small detailed propositions for education. I would suggest it might be a good idea to channel them through a single minister of the crown. I am not suggesting that one minister should have the responsibility of initiating all such measures; I am not suggesting that one minister should be responsible for dealing with all such measures,
The Address-Mr. Enfield but I do suggest that there be one gathering point where the public and hon. members could look at a list and see just what is being done, what is being spent and where it is being spent.
I do not think this list shows much of a trend in so far as the division or separating of this money is concerned. There is one grant to universities made by the Department of Finance which amounts to some $8 million, and which now presumably will amount to something like $16 million. This is based on a formula so far as the division of the money is concerned, but that is not so with the rest of these expenditures. I make this suggestion because the public in inquiring of the federal government as to what is available for education must find it most difficult to ascertain just what is taking place.
Coming back to the province, if I may take just one or two more minutes on this subject, it has been suggested that there should be further aid for education. At one time the province of Ontario agreed to pay to the municipalities 50 per cent of the cost of education. I have obtained some figures of the actual grants, and I find that in 1945 the province to the municipalities paid some 54 per cent of those costs for education. I find also that in 1954-55 the grants for education by the province of Ontario came to some 34 per cent of the moneys spent by municipalities for that purpose.
This is quite a drastic change. What is the reason? We do not know. We are being asked to provide more money for education without any explanation of why this proposed division of the cost of education as between the province and the municipalities has broken down. Is it that educational costs have risen too steeply? Is it that the revenues of the province have not been so controlled as to increase in the manner in which they should? Is the province not sufficiently taxing certain industries-the mines, perhaps, and the lumbering and forest industry? Are the revenues not sufficiently stable and equitable from all sources in the province? We do not know the answers to those questions, and we cannot exercise proper and good judgment in regard to these constant requests for educational aid unless they are answered properly by the provinces and the municipalities.
These are my submissions in the throne speech debate. I venture to suggest that when the vote is taken in the next few days the government will receive a resounding vote of confidence in regard to its activities.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The Address-Mr. Nickle AFTER RECESS
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I extend the usual congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Next, I should like to extend my warm personal congratulations to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) on his election to the high office of leader of the party of which I am a member. The hon. member for Prince Albert follows a long line of illustrious leaders of the Conservative party in Canada, and I know will be making a notably great contribution as leader of the Conservative party and as a prime minister of Canada in the years ahead.
At the same time, sir, may I express my deep personal regrets at the enforced retirement of Hon. George Drew as leader of my party due to ill health. Mr. Drew made a notable contribution to our country, to the party which he led and to parliament itself during his many years in office.
My main purpose tonight is to review the recent past and the near-term future of the great new Canadian industry which makes its headquarters in Calgary. I refer, of course, to western Canada's oil and gas industry, which has made Calgary one of the two fastest growing cities in Canada and earned for my home city the title of Canada's oil capital.
Before doing that I have a few comments to make concerning the C.P.R. strike, which is having a serious effect upon every phase of Canada's economy. In the west grain shipments have slowed down, aggravating the problems of our great agricultural industry which provides the broad base of the western economy. In a number of manufacturing industries in Alberta and elsewhere in the west cut-backs in production and in employment are already in effect because of the C.P.R. strike, and the situation will become far more serious over the next few days unless the strike is settled among industries dependent upon the C.P.R. for the transport of raw materials and finished products.
On strike are some 3,000 members of the firemen's union over the issue of whether or not firemen should be retained on diesel-powered freight and yard engines. The issue might also be summed up in this way. Should the railways and their workers keep pace with other industries and their workers in the trend toward automation and greater efficiency, consistent with adequate safety measures, in a world and especially in a country like Canada where competition in


trade and in transport is tight and where manpower to build the future is in short supply?
Only 3,000 are on strike, but over 70,000 C.P.R. employees are off the payroll as a result of the complete shut-down the strike involves. Rapidly increasing thousands of non-railwaymen are losing jobs in other industries because of the strike. The cost to Canada's economy and to every citizen of our country grows heavier every hour.
This government has shown little willingness so far to face up to the real issue involved, to put the interests of all of Canada ahead of any other consideration and get the C.P.R. back in operation by application of firm and courageous government policy. The government seems to be relying upon public opinion to push it into action and to determine the specific kind of action that should be taken.
Back in 1950 the Conservative group in the house proposed the improvement and modernization of the machinery for the conciliation of industrial disputes. The government voted down the proposal. Since then neither labour nor management has known with any certainty the government's labour dispute policies. Certainly there has been no government policy in so far as the effective handling of problems arising from automation and changing industrial trends are concerned. Issues such as wages or working conditions between labour and management can ordinarily be resolved by normal conciliation or bargaining practices. But can the same be said for issues such as automation, technological changes, related safety measures and so forth? Why has not this government, knowing full well that considerations other than wages and other normal matters of difference existed so far as the C.P.R. and the firemen's union were concerned, taken adequate steps in advance of this tragic strike to create machinery for the proper resolving by an authority independent of the two sides to the dispute of the matters at issue?
Certainly the basic point of dispute between the firemen's union and the railway is one that cannot possibly be solved by a strike, for a strike, regardless of which side wins out, does not and cannot resolve in equity and fairness the merits and demerits of automation or safety measures which are at issue. Regardless of where our individual sympathies may lie as between the railway and union positions, the majority of Canadians at least recognize that the issue is a somewhat technical one calling for the application of careful study on an unbiased basis by a qualified commission. Both sides

to the dispute in fact agree to that extent. So also to that extent does the government now seem to agree in its position as representative of the most vitally interested party of all, the general public of Canada.
Speaking as an individual member of parliament and in no other capacity, I say to both the union and the C.P.R. management: If you believe your case is right, if you believe it can stand up under the harsh light of critical examination by a competent, unbiased public board, then back your faith now by voluntarily agreeing to present all the facts and arguments to that unbiased board and to abide by the decision of that board. I refer to the technical issue of the need or lack of it for firemen on diesel engines for efficient operation, and the related technical issue of adequate safety measures for rail-waymen, property and the public. In the meantime, restore the status quo and get the railway back in operation.
To the government I say this: Show more courage and leadership than you have to date to get Canada back on the rails. Quit waiting for public opinion to force you into decisive action on this particular problem and the far broader question of modernized government machinery to assist in the fair and equitable resolving of technological problems such as those now facing Canada, plus much better machinery for the resolving without compulsion of the more normal differences on wages and other matters which arise from time to time between labour and management.
The Conservative party back in 1950 and at various times since has given the government a sound basis for a better labour dispute policy. I urge the government to end its dilly-dallying by concrete action now. Or are we on this side of the house and the Canadian public generally to assume that the government has not solved the railway problem but has quietly helped to relieve Canada's shortage of steel for industry by giving away that steel that should have been retained in the collective government backbone?
Departing from the railroad strike, I should like to make a few comments on the western Canadian oil and gas industry, give a brief review of the past and take a look at the present and the near-term future for what has become Canada's No. 1 mineral-producing industry and western Canada's No. 2 industry, second, of course, to agriculture in terms of revenue and employment.
First let me deal with revenue. In 1956 this industry in western Canada poured out a record $404 million worth of crude oil and other liquid petroleum products, an average of about $1,122,000 a day. In the current
The Address-Mr. Nickle year, 1957, production revenues should climb to substantially over half a billion dollars. The rate of growth is all the more remarkable when we consider that in 1947, a decade ago, when the Leduc discovery set off the boom, production amounted to only $18 million yearly. By 1955 it had climbed to $307 million for that year, and rose by a third again in 1956.
Offsetting the revenue is investment. Into the western Canadian economy in 1956 the host of members-hundreds of them-of the oil and gas industry pumped an investment of around $700 million for exploration, development, land, pipe lines and refineries, an amount far in excess of the former record of just over a half a billion dollars set in 1955. A decade ago the investment rate was only $12 million yearly. In 1957 over-all investment should come close to the 1956 record, with gas and oil pipe-line construction helping to offset some curtailment in exploration and development spendings.
Along with revenue and investment, of course, has come production. In terms of oil production, the normal rate of growth has been accelerated in recent months by the Middle East crisis which has forced a reshuffling of world oil supply lines to offset the closing of the Suez canal in Egypt, the closing of three of the four oil pipe lines crossing Syria to the Mediterranean, and Saudi Arabia's embargo on its oil deliveries to British and French markets. Canada's role in this crisis, so far as oil is concerned, has been and is delivery of its oil to various North American and Asian markets in order to free Venezuelan and United States gulf coast oil for delivery to hard-pressed Europe.
Largely because of offshore shipments from Vancouver to California and Japan, and increased deliveries to the United States midwest, western Canada's oil production climbed to an average of 509,000 barrels daily during the final quarter of 1956, which was about
52.000	barrels a day more than during the first nine months of the year. The net result of this was a 1956 daily average production of
470.000	barrels, which was about 110,000 barrels a day more than that of 1955.
During the first quarter of 1957 production is expected to advance a further 58,000 barrels a day over the late 1956 rate to around
567.000	barrels daily, and to hold around this level until the final quarter of the year, when additions to pipe lines and refinery facilities will permit a step-up to somewhere between
623.000	barrels and 658,000 barrels per day.
The actual volume late this year will depend a good deal on the speed with which world oil supply lines and ocean transport costs are restored to normalcy. Normalcy,

The Address-Mr. Nickle however, will not involve loss by Canada of the production gains it is registering during the present emergency; for the growing hunger in North America, and the probable adoption by the United States of a continental oil policy, will leave Canadian oil relatively free to expand its markets in both Canadian and American areas within economic reach. A continental policy for oil and gas, which I have long advocated in this house, has been winning support in such vital bodies as the United States office of defence mobilization as a result of the impact of the Middle East oil crisis.
A measure of the importance of western Canadian oil to the nation and to the free world is given by the fact that in early 1957, just one decade since Leduc's discovery, production will be running at a rate 30 times greater than that of 10 years ago, and during this year daily yield will increase by a further amount three to five times greater than our west's entire production of pre-Leduc days.
Mr. Speaker, production also involves a matter of price. Along with the oil supply crisis, particularly in Europe, the Middle East situation has brought some fantastic boosts in oil transport costs by tanker, throwing the normal competitive factors of world oil pricing out of kilter. Markets for western hemisphere oil have been tightening as the result of big boosts in production to help supply Europe. These factors have directly brought on in recent weeks increases in wellhead prices for oil in Venezuela, California and the United States midwest, and in the past week have brought on a general increase averaging 35 cents per barrel in Texas, Louisiana and the other major United States producing states. These increases are somewhat less than might have applied if the full rise in ocean transport costs were taken into account.
This general rise in United States oil prices in the past few days will likely bring on an increase in western Canadian oil prices in the immediate future, probably somewhere in the range between 20 cents and 30 cents per barrel. The Canadian oil price structure is tied competitively to that of the United States, whose oil is the alternative supply for the major markets in North America where our oil competes. The United States held oil prices in major areas constant for the last three years until last week, despite rising costs of industry operation, wages, steel and so forth, while Canadian producers had gradually to reduce their wellhead prices in order to expand their marketing area. Now the move will be in the opposite direction. Incidentally, western Canadian oil prices will continue to be around 10 per cent to 12 per cent lower than wellhead prices in the major

United States producing areas. The higher crude oil costs will likely mean about one cent per gallon increase in gasoline and other petroleum products costs in the United States and Canada. These boosts started in the United States last week, and likely will start in Canada very shortly.
An extremely important point about the growth of this industry has been the growth of oil exports. Exports of our western Canadian oil to foreign markets, mainly in contiguous areas of the United States, more than doubled in 1956 to an average of over 112,500 barrels daily, compared to only 51,000 barrels daily in 1955 and only 8,000 barrels daily in 1954, when exports commenced. United States dollar payments for the 1956 exports are estimated at nearly $120 million for the 40 million barrels moved beyond Canada's borders, thus putting oil into the top half dozen of foreign exchange earners for Canada.
During 1957 Canada's oil exports are expected nearly to double again, and should average at least 198,000 barrels daily for this year, but may run as high as 213,000 barrels. During the early part of this year exports should average 185,000 barrels daily, and will climb as more transport and processing facilities become available, perhaps reaching as high as a quarter of a million barrels later this year.
The greater volume of export, plus some rise in price levels, may make our western oil in 1957 a quarter billion dollar foreign exchange earner. Fully a third of Canada's 1957 production will find its way to foreign markets, with as much as 10,000 barrels daily on an average going to Japan, and the balance to the United States Pacific coast and midwest areas. Canada's rapidly rising foreign exchange return from oil exports, and the continuing heavy inflow of foreign capital for natural resource development, are vital factors in preventing a grave worsening of Canada's imbalance between exports and imports.
During recent months the Middle East crisis eliminated the cushion in pipe-line transport capacity east and west from our oil territory, as demand for oil brought capacity into full use. The crisis also speeded up plans for expansion of transport systems, particularly by the Trans Mountain pipe line across the Rockies. A looping program will start this year that could, within two to three years, bring a complete second parallel oil line to the Pacific. The Interprovincial pipe line running east from Alberta will be extended this summer from Sarnia into Toronto, tying in with refinery expansion at Toronto to permit Canadian oil to displace foreign oil

in a larger share of the eastern Ontario market. Interprovincial will also complete its looping program across the prairies this year, to enable winter deliveries by the year end to both eastern Canada and the United States midwest.
In 1957-58 there will be greater expansion of certain Canadian refineries using western Canadian oil, further contributing to the growth of this vital Canadian industry. But the biggest single market boost over the next three years is going to be the United States Pacific northwest. Here construction will start this year of at least two major refineries with a capacity totalling over 100,000 barrels daily and one or two more will likely start construction soon after.
Of course we cannot consider oil without touching also on natural gas. The first major export of western Canadian natural gas, Mr. Speaker, to both Canadian and United States markets will actually commence in the second half of this year. Thus will come the start of the realization of dreams and plans in existence for nearly nine years, since the first gas pipe line was proposed and started running into political and economic roadblocks. The flow of gas from the Peace river region of Alberta and British Columbia will start this summer through the first completed major gas line, Westcoast Transmission Company's 650-mile line across the Rockies to Vancouver and the United States border, where it will connect with the recently completed Pacific Northwest pipe-line system. Gas from southern Alberta will start its movement eastward this year through the prairie sections of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines system, and during 1958-59 will probably reach into eastern Canada and the midwest United States in large volume.
Westcoast licked its major problems in 1956. It completed adequate gas sales contracts in British Columbia and the United States, successfully completed its financing and started construction. The line is now 70 per cent completed, and construction will be completed this spring and summer, with operation to start by late summer. In the meantime, through the Pacific Northwest pipe line United States gas is now reaching Vancouver. This flow will be reversed when Westcoast completes its Peace river line.
Within the next three weeks Trans-Canada Pipe Lines will launch the public financing of its 2,250-mile system, with reasonable assurance that the financing will be successful. One of the company's toughest economic problems, the politically-dictated all-Canadian route through 1,000 miles of limited-market Northern Ontario, was offset last spring by the Ontario-federal government 82715-8
The Address-Mr. Nickle plan covering that section of the system to ease the financial strain during the early tough years of market build-up. The other problem, access to United States midwest markets to provide revenue to help carry the Canadian system at lowest possible gas costs to Canadian consumers, is still being battled out before the United States federal power commission, but it is now fairly evident that mutual Canadian-United States economic and defence interests ensure that access will be obtained in the relatively near future, either in the form presently proposed or in some modification of it.
During 1956, with the help of short-term advances from the Canadian government, Trans-Canada started construction of its system across Saskatchewan and Manitoba, but the United States steel strike held back pipe deliveries and prevented completion to Winnipeg before the onset of winter halted construction. By then 227 miles of pipe line had been completed. Construction will resume this spring as soon as weather permits, and gas should be as far as Winnipeg late this summer. In the meantime, Trans-Canada has successfully completed arrangements for the sale of its senior bonds to United States and Canadian insurance companies, subject to certain revisions in its gas purchase contract demanded by a key insurance firm. By this week contracts for over 80 per cent of the gas had been renegotiated in line with these requirements, and the balance will probably be completed shortly.
The new terms involved no change in prices to be paid for gas, but do involve changes in volumes committed for by Trans-Canada on a take or pay basis. They involve an additional hardship for gas producers on top of that imposed by the fairly low start in prices dictated by the all-Canadian route, but are accepted by producers as part of the price they must pay to help free Canadian gas from its shackles and thus speed the building of a great new phase of the Canadian oil and gas industry. To the extent that they are ready and willing to do so, Canadians across the nation will have their biggest single opportunity to date to invest in a major gas or oil transport system when Trans-Canada's public offer is made within the next three weeks. The offering will total $120 million, including $40 million in common stock and $80 million in junior bonds set up in a stock-bond package.
Canadians can, if they desire, buy a substantial majority of the total equity stock to be issued by Trans-Canada on terms comparable to those under which capital has been subscribed by the several major and independent oil and gas firms who are

The Address-Mr. Nickle Trans-Canada's present shareholders. The same opportunity will be extended soon after, primarily to Alberta citizens, in the financing of the Alberta gas trunk pipe line which will gather gas in Alberta for delivery to Trans-Canada at the Saskatchewan border.
Neither of these, sir, are get rich quick schemes, but they do appear to have a fairly solid long-term future. They represent not only a good, long-term opportunity to share Canada's future, but also a definite challenge to those Canadians critical of a heavy foreign capital flavour in Canadian resource development, and those who have decried what they term a shortage of opportunities for Canadians to invest in and control major resource projects. The coming two projects alone will give Canadians in 1957 more than $160 million worth of such opportunity. I trust they will avail themselves of it and hold their investment, rather than let the securities drift away to foreign investors who have faith in Canada's future.
Part and parcel of large-scale gas exports, Mr. Speaker-and just as important from western Canada's point of view-is the building and operation of gas processing plants, sulphur recovery plants and related chemical plants in the gas-source fields in nearby communities. In anticipation of West-coast's pipe line, Canadians and Americans joined in 1956 to start construction in the Peace river area of British Columbia of a $30 million gas, sulphur and refinery project. This, the first large industrial operation of its kind in British Columbia, is slated to go into production this summer.
In anticipation of Trans-Canada's pipe line, and to open a source of sulphur supply to the big new nitro-chemical plant built by Canadian and United States interests at Medicine Hat in 1956, the owners of the Pincher Creek gas field completed recently the first phases in southwest Alberta of what will become in years ahead Canada's largest gas processing and sulphur project. As dry gas needs of Trans-Canada and Westcoast expand into more of the currently shut-in gas fields of the west, there will be a host of new plants for the extraction of natural gasoline, propane, butane and sulphur from the fields to be put to use. During this year it is probable that several more such projects will be announced, particularly in south and central Alberta.
I should like now to briefly refer to exploration and development in the west. In 1956, for the first time in history, more than 3,000 wells were completed in western Canada. Some 3,287 wells gave their answer, 400 more than in 1955, and 1,000 more than


in 1954. Of these 2,360 completions were for oil wells, 190 were gas wells and there were 737 which were dry holes or failures which are inevitable in exploration.
This year will be another big year so far as exploration and development are concerned, but a number of factors indicate that it will fall short of 1956 in terms of new capital invested in those phases of industry spendings and in terms of well completions. These factors include first of all the present tight money situation and higher interest rates which hit particularly, so far as oil is concerned, at capital-seeking independents, though of course not even major firms are immune. Second, our Canadian taxation laws, which are less favourable than United States laws in respect to depletion and certain other write-offs, tend to mitigate against Canadian companies in resource development here, and will tend also in the near future to divert United States capital and also Canadian capital to United States development rather than into Canadian projects. I trust that the recommendations made today in the Gordon report, if carried out fast enough, will have a favourable result in offsetting the present outlook so far as tax laws affecting development of our resources are concerned.
A third factor in this year's development is something of fairly recent origin, namely rulings by Canadian tax collectors reclassifying some forms of presumed tax-free capital gains as capital income in the hands of a number of oil men and investors. This has definitely discouraged a number of affected operators who have long been prominent in Canadian oil and gas development. For the benefit of my C.C.F. friends, may I say I am not one of those affected.
The fourth point is the recent sharp curtailment in Middle East oil income going to international oil companies, which is now having some effect on their 1957 budget planning for their Canadian as well as other areas of development.
The fifth point is the fact that there is some diversion of funds from exploration and development because of the high capital requirements for refinery and transport system.
The final point affecting capital for development has been the generally unfavourable levels in 1956 of United States-Canadian oil and gas prices which, incidentally, are lower in Canada than in the United States. Those did not advance during the year to offset rises in wages, steel and other material costs. It is now expected, however, that the price situation will generally improve this year,

as it started to do in the United States last week and will likely start to do in Canada in the immediate future.
In the two or three minutes remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly, since I have dealt with Western Canada as a whole, on the major areas of promise in the west. Alberta, of course, has been and still is Canada's top oil and gas province. By the end of 1956 Alberta boosted its oil production to around 426,000 barrels a day, and will climb from around 450,000 barrels a day, today, to probably over half a million barrels a day by the end of the year.
In 1956 Saskatchewan clinched its position as the second most important oil-producing province in Canada. Saskatchewan had a long string of oil discoveries in the southeastern section of the province, and they have already established over a hundred million barrels of reserves. The new southeast Saskatchewan area has combined with the older southwest area to bring about a skyrocketing of Saskatchewan oil production. That production almost doubled last year to an average of over 53,000 barrels a day. They started off in 1957 with over 75,000 barrels a day, and within the next three or four months Saskatchewan will be producing in excess of 100,000 barrels a day.
Manitoba, the third ranking province, showed some increase during the year. Its production built up during the year from
11,000	to about 17,000 barrels a day. There has been no notable discovery during the year, but prospects are quite bright.
British Columbia during 1956 produced its first oil, and by the end of the year passed its first milestone of 1,000 barrels a day. During the current year British Columbia will greatly increase its importance as an oil-producing area and will also, of course, begin to come into its own as a major supplier of natural gas and by-products.
The Northwest Territories, which possesses Canada's most northerly oil field, Norman Wells, continued during last year to meet the needs of the mining and transport operations in the Northwest Territories, namely around 1,100 barrels a day. There are at the present time several million acres of territory containing mineral rights currently held by large oil and mineral companies in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and during the year and in the years ahead a great deal of money will be expended by industry, not only to untap but to unlock some of these large resources of oil, gas and other minerals which most competent observers now believe to exist in the northern reaches of our country.
