speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I would not want to miss the opportunity to congratulate sincerely the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, because they have both shown themselves worthy of their constituents and I have no doubt that they will soon be given unmistakable evidence of appreciation.
I intend to deal with certain problems of special concern to my constituency, one of which is mentioned in the speech from the throne, that is "greater encouragement to the farmers", and to make a few suggestions concerning the application of the unemployment insurance act.
Representing a constituency that is exclusively agricultural, I consider that the interest shown by the present government in these numerous problems facing our farmers must be implemented by measures whose application will soon have salutary effects; otherwise, within ten years we shall witness a substantial reduction of the present number of: operating farms.
The farmer's income must remain at least equal to the average of that of other trades, and agriculture must offer advantages at least equal to those enjoyed by Canadian workers, generally.
Our farmers hold with reason that too often their products merely cover their expenses. The uncertainty of obtaining adequate prices ior their products has the effect of discouraging private initiative.
On many farms, the farmers have been making a living out of lumbering as well as from the sale of the usual farm products. On many farms the timber stands are depleted, and the farmer loses half of his income sources. If the farmer is not helped and guided in his production, he will tend to seek another way of life. His status as owner will be changed to that of an employee offering his services to industry. There follow from this a number of serious consequences for the survival of the agricultural class in this country; unemployment, removal to cities and the loss of an important part of our national heritage, a part which is as essential to the progress of this country as every great phase of our industrial development.

The Address-Mr. Laflamme
Among the necessary remedies besides reforestation we must include planned production and the assurance given these fellow citizens of ours that their labours will be recompensed by stable markets and a remuneration sufficiently large to allow them to earn their living in as much comfort at least as other classes of Canadian workers.
I would also like to bring to the Minister of Finance's (Mr. Harris) attention and to the attention too of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) a request already made by the Catholic Farmers' Union, and which I consider highly justified. They ask that farm revenue be considered as the result of a family enterprise and not as the fruit of the work of the father only.
At the present time a farmer who works the land with his sons must pay income tax on the whole of the revenue unless he has paid his sons in cash.
It must not be forgotten that the father who is a farmer is the head of a family undertaking. The work of the children is the source of his revenue and even if this work is not paid in cash, it can legitimately be argued that it should be deducted from the personal income of the father. Should the father wish to remunerate the work accomplished by his sons, he would have to pay considerable salaries which would reduce his income and which would be deductible from his income tax under present arrangements.
Child labour, whether paid for in cash or not, should also be legitimately deducted from the revenue of the whole farm since revenue due to the work of a large number of people should not be taxed as revenue earned by only one person. The father-son relationship should not constitute an exception to this rule.
I now wish to call the attention of the house to the present situation as far as unemployment insurance is concerned.
I am going to make but a few suggestions which, I believe, could appreciably improve the administration of the unemployment insurance act and regulations.
It should always be borne in mind that, and I believe that it is the purpose of this law, the unemployed is in most cases in urgent need of an income.
The great number of insurance claims may seem normal to the officer dealing with the claims, but a quick settlement of the cases submitted is essential to the unemployed.
In my opinion a further decentralization of the insurance offices is required, as in some periods of the year they are overworked, and cannot, in spite of the co-operation of the staff, deal adequately with the claims submitted.

Also the unemployed person should not have to travel several miles at his own expense in order to submit his claim or to obtain the information he wants.
A larger number of offices would meet that need more adequately.
A good many claimants often need information either about the way they should submit their claim or about the administration of the act, the regulations under which are amended almost every year. It is essential, I think, that any unemployed person applying to an unemployment office to fill in his application forms be met by someone in a position to give him all the information required, to acquaint him with the benefits provided by law and to interpret the act in connection with the facts stated by the applicant.
Often the commission sends by mail to the applicant a set of questions with which he is unable to deal adequately. However, the answers are taken literally and sometimes result in unjustified disqualifications.
Surely all these worries suffered by the applicant could be avoided by a more thorough study of the case at the outset.
In the event of an appeal from the decisions of the insurance officer, the appellant, in most cases, must go to a lawyer. If he wins his case, the commission returns him his benefits but makes no allowance whatever for his travelling expenses and does not even pay the fees of the person who helped him state his case.
In my opinion, this is not normal. Either the commission must provide free of charge the services of a lawyer, in such a case, or it should have in its own office someone who would act in all cases as counsel for the claimants and would at all times be at their disposal. This is the procedure followed in connection with the pensions and allowances of war veterans.
Moreover, I would suggest that a lawyer sit on every conciliation board made up of three (3) members since, in fact, the function of these boards is to pass judgment on the legality of a claim and to analyse the facts in accordance with the spirit of the act. The decisions at present made by these boards are based, 95 per cent of the time, on cases already heard. Such decisions make up a jurisprudence while we all know that each case may have characteristics of its own.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, I suggest:
1.	That a larger number of offices be established so as to be within reach of the unemployed and thus avoid large travelling expenses.

2.	That employees responsible for supplying information and acting, so to speak, as counsel for the claimant be posted in each office.
3.	That costs be paid to each claimant who succeeds in gaining his point before the board of arbitration.
4.	That a lawyer be named on each board of arbitration.
All this should be done in order to lend a greater efficiency to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which is so essential to the workers, to ensure better relations between claimants and commission employees, and to make people aware that unemployment insurance, which is paid by the government, by the employers and by the employees is a capital guarantee for the workers to whom it gives collective security in case of unemployment.
My fellow-citizens always look to the future with confidence and they remain confident that their demands will always be heard more favourably by the present government than under any other system of government.
The legislation enacted by the government in the social security field and gigantic projects such as the St. Lawrence seaway and the construction of a trans-Canada pipe line set the pace for our industrial development and stimulate private enterprise. We can safely say that our people enjoy the highest standard of living in the world, after our neighbours to the south.
Enjoying an enviable reputation, having a truly Canadian foreign policy, we will soon see the day, I hope, when our Canadianism will be attested by a national emblem which will remain a symbol of unity, and of a desire for peace and freedom.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deem it a great privilege to be able to voice once again in this House of Commons what I believe are the sentiments of the people of my constituency. I regret the need to mention once again some of the problems that face the people back home. I had hoped that a large number of these problems which already existed when I was first elected in 1953 would have been met by adequate legislation on the part of this parliament by this date; however, the government has not seen fit to meet these needs thus far.
There are a great many problems that cause us some concern, but in one short talk one cannot begin to deal with all of them. I would like very much to deal with the problem of housing, which threatens to become a most serious problem this year. I would also like to speak on the subject of insurance in all its phases. When I look at the statistics that are available I see the
The Address-Mr. Regier Canadian people are bleeding themselves white in a vain effort to buy for themselves a feeling of security in this rich Canada of ours. I would like, too, to raise the problems^, confronting the Canadian veteran, and E would also like to speak concerning the problems of the British Columbia farmer. I do* feel, however, there are two problems which are most urgent at the present time, and I intend to confine my remarks to these two matters.
I think the greatest problem facing the people, in my constituency at least, is the need for an upward revision in the old age. pension. I believe I am safe in saying that, there are not many constituencies in Canada; in which reside over 7,000 old age pensioners. Almost every fourth or fifth person I meet when I am home is under old age security benefits.
The other problem I have in mind is the failure of the federal government of Canada to recognize adequately other levels of government in Canada. I do not use the term "lower levels of government" because that would be reflecting the attitude of the government of Canada. In my estimation the other governments of Canada are not in any way lower governments, and I feel it is time that we put an end to people referring to municipal and provincial governments and other forms of organized society as lower levels of government.
I listened closely, and the following day I read closely, the speech from the throne, but failed to find an indication that those two major problems are being tackled by the proposals offered by the government. I see recorded on page 2 of Hansard such expressions as "excellent progress", "expansion", "rapid strides", "unprecedented levels", "blessed", "greater" and "enjoying the benefits". In one paragraph almost every sentence contains an adjective or superlative to indicate the wonderful blessings we have in Canada, the inference of course being while under a Liberal regime.
I dare say that may be so in a good many respects, and I do not want to take away any credit for progress where progress has been made. In my estimation the speech from the throne consists of 75 per cent pious platitudes, 20 per cent references to minor legislation and amendments of detail, and 5 per cent reference to some of the problems with which Canadians will be faced. In that 5 per cent I would include the reference to the setting up of a Canada Council, an increase in grants to universities, increases and extensions of grants to technical and vocational education,

The Address-Mr. Regier an amendment to the Municipal Grants Act, and the continuation of the wheat board as the sole marketing agency.
This is a long way from meeting some of the problems faced by our people, many of which have been caused directly by the progress we have been making in certain fields. My greatest complaint and the greatest complaint of old age pensioners is that the prosperity of Canada is not being shared equitably by all sections of the Canadian people. I think if old age pensioners read that one paragraph beginning with "excellent progress" and containing such expressions as "expansion", "rapid strides", "unprecedented levels" and so on, they would find such boasting slightly nauseating, almost as nauseating as the gas which unfortunately many of them turn on at night in order to put an end to the miserable existence they are forced to face.
The C.C.F. proposal in regard to old age pensions has been for long $65 a month at age 65 without a means test. In addition we have proposed on numerous occasions, and in the province of Saskatchewan where the C.C.F. forms the government we have implemented, a program of health care for old age pensioners. We have advocated on more than one occasion-and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has referred to this in the house-low rental housing for our senior citizens and others with similar low incomes.
An old age pension of $65 a month at age 65 in British Columbia, if we retained the present $20 supplementary payment by the provincial government with a means test, would mean that the needy people of our province would have an income of $85 per month. That would go a long way toward making those people feel that they too were enjoying some of the benefits of this rich Canada which they had helped to build.
I want to pay a compliment to another relatively new political party in Canada upon the attitude it has taken on the subject of old age pensions, and I refer to the Social Credit party. I feel that in the three western provinces we have gone a long way toward alleviating some of the suffering of these people, and we fail to understand why a rich province such as Ontario cannot do at least as well as Saskatchewan, under a C.C.F. government, or Alberta and British Columbia, and pay a $20 supplementary allowance.
I regret that I cannot go along with the proposals which have received publicity in our daily press back home and which have been made by the Social Credit government in British Columbia. According to the press
IMr. Regier.]

reports they are advocating that Ottawa continue to pay $40 a month but agree to share the cost of the supplementary allowance on a 50-50 basis. If I have misunderstood the proposal I hope that succeeding speakers will correct me, but I understand that this would mean $80 per month in British Columbia, which almost equals $85.
However, we in our group are sufficiently aware of the problems faced by other parts of Canada to realize that while such a proposal might be satisfactory to the rich provinces of Canada, there are many provinces that would be unable to meet that type of matching grant arrangement. If such an arrangement were to be adopted by this government it would mean that once again we would have old age pensioners in one part of Canada receiving much less than those in other parts.
The other day someone asked me how much I thought old age pensions in Canada should be. The C.C.F. and many other major non-political organizations have advocated $65 at 65 without a means test, but my answer to that question was that in reality it is very difficult to say offhand how much an old age pension should be. My answer would be that the least we could do is to bring the purchasing power of the old age pension back to what it was in 1927. I submit that $40 does not supply to our senior citizens today those things which they have to buy to the extent that $20 did back in 1927. It may be that the value of our money has been reduced by about that percentage, but when we consider the things on which these people spend their money we are today on a much lower level than we were back when old age pensions were first introduced. That purchasing power, as I said, should be restored, and in addition I feel that the senior citizens of Canada should also share in the technological advances and the great increase in production of our Canadian economy. They are as entitled as anyone else to an ever-rising standard of living.
The first essential, of course, when we advocate an increase in the old age pension, is that we must establish the need for an increase. I do not think I have to say very much on that point. Our government recognizes, and I am in full accord with what they are doing in this respect, that our newly-arriving immigrants from Hungary must be maintained at government expense for some time until they can be fully established. However, what is the estimate of this expense? As I understand the situation, the government is prepared, where necessary, to pay up to $3 a day for the maintenance of a refugee from Hungary. I want to make it very clear that I do not oppose that in any

way. The C.C.F. party was the first to criticize the government for not doing enough for would-be immigrants to Canada.
However, we can easily understand the feeling of our senior citizens when they are told that they must exist on $1.33 a day in a country they have helped to build and for whose wealth they are responsible when the same country can turn around and, after ignoring their needs, can pay for the maintenance of other people the sum of $3 per day. It seems rather inequitable. With respect to the need, where do we find these senior citizens who need an increase in the old age pension so badly? Sometimes they are rather difficult to find. They cannot afford to live on the ground floor level with the street. You have to go up to third and fourth floor attic rooms to find them. You have to go into musty basement rooms to find them. You have to go to the shacks on the outskirts of the better residential areas. When we consider the conditions under which our senior citizens are forced to live in many parts of Canada I believe that some of us should hang our heads in shame.
What can you buy today on $40 a month? You go to various homes in our cities and you find that the average modest room in an old dilapidated rooming house will cost you $30 a month. That leaves our old age pensioner with the magnificent sum of $10 a month with which to pay for food, clothing, in many cases medical care, and all the other necessities of life. I know I am not speaking of the average citizen in Canada today. However, there are over 100,000 old age pensioners in the province of British Columbia alone to whom this is an important issue.
I know that some of the people of Canada have been enjoying relatively good times ever since world war II began. I know there are some Canadians, and I meet some of them rather often, who as a hobby are able to afford farms in the country. They would not dare attempt to make a living from their farms; otherwise we might get some decent farm legislation. You know, it is lovely to be able to take your guests on a Sunday to the farm or ranch. Some of these people keep horses there, or cattle and other livestock. I have seen some of the stables. It is very nice to be able to show your guests around. But in carrying out these hobbies far more money is being spent on housing for the horses and cattle than is being spent on housing, food and clothing for people who have helped to develop this country and who are responsible for some being able to have farms as a hobby where they can go on a Sunday, and maybe by having such farms help to relieve the income tax situation.
The Address-Mr. Regier
It is not the fault of these old people that they are in such great need. Not only are they in great need, but so are our blind pensioners, our veterans and our disabled people. In referring to our old age pensioners I have in mind all people who have to exist on pensions paid by the people of Canada through the government. I almost made the mistake of saying "paid by the government". The money is paid by the people of Canada through the government.
Many little things can be done to make the lives of many people easier. We still insist on the cruel 20-year residence clause. You do not have to be a citizen in order to obtain the $40 a month. You can be a foreigner. You need never have made any major contribution to Canadian citizenship and the welfare of the Canadian community as a whole. You need have no citizenship papers, but if you have lived here for 20 years you are entitled to the $40 a month. However, if you were a refugee from Hitlerism in the Sudetenland and came here in 1939 because you were a believer in democracy and your life was at stake, then even though you may be as old as Methuselah this government will not have any mercy on you because you have not lived here for 20 years. If you are in need you have to go and beg assistance from the local municipal welfare office.
I think it is high time that we removed the 20-year residence requirement. When our own citizens are given a rawer deal than people who may have lived here for a long time but have never assumed the responsibilities of citizenship, I think something should be done.
The question then arises, can we afford $65 a month at 65 for everyone in Canada, plus free health care and plus low rental housing for these people? In 1927 the gross national product of Canada was a little under $6 billion. In 1956 it was over $29 billion, and for this year the forecast is over $30 billion. In other words our gross national product has gone up five times since 1927. If we could afford to pay $20 a month then it is not too illogical to conclude that we should be able to pay $100 a month now, or five times what we paid then.
Looking at the matter in another way and going back only to 1949, when the universal $40 pension was introduced, at that time the gross national product of Canada amounted to $16.4 billion. This year we expect it to be practically twice as much. On the basis of a gross national product of $16.4 billion we decided the economy could afford a pension of $40 a month. Surely when our production
112	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Regier is twice as high the economy should be able to afford twice as high a pension. That would be $80 a month.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. proposals turn out to be most reasonable indeed. I receive letters in my mail asking me to plead for a pension of $100 a month. 1 am not saying that Canada cannot afford to pay $100 a month. However, if the government would pay $65 a month at 65 I know it would go a long way toward meeting the urgent need in Canada. We are responsible to a very great extent for the financial position in which these people find themselves. By deliberate policy the government has permitted the inflation of our currency over a long period of years, thereby indirectly-it may seem very direct to those affected-robbing hundreds of thousands of our senior citizens of what they thought was an adequate retirement plan for which they had sacrificed. Many of them had purchased annuities. Many of them had done it through life insurance company investments. Many of them had done it through investment in farms and the like.
There were a great many who lost their assets during the catastrophe of the hungry thirties. There are many in my riding who lost their farms on the prairies because of the economic conditions at that time. This parliament at that time passed emergency legislation to safeguard the apparent solvency of the investment houses and insurance companies of Canada, but this parliament did nothing to safeguard the solvency of the vast majority of the producers of Canada, at that time notably the farmers of the western plains. I have many of them in my riding who, under normal circumstances, would have been able to look after themselves in their old age in their own way and would have done so very well.
That is why I say this parliament shares a great measure of responsibility for the need that now exists. Not all the proposed increase will be net cost to government. Much of this money returns into the hands of the various governments of Canada. By means of sales and excise taxes, customs duties and, in the case of those who do not need it, income tax and succession duties, a goodly share of this money is returned and is therefore not a net loss to government income.
I also think of the great aid this would be to Canadian agriculture. When these old age pensioners get more money, what will they do with it? They will go out into the market place and maybe for once be able to buy a few eggs, a little bit of bacon, some butter, some cheese and so on. That is what our farmers need. They need a market
[Mr. Regier.l

at home in Canada. Paying more money to the old age and other pensioners of Canada is the easiest way of relieving at least some of the problems of Canadian agriculture.
I do not plead, Mr. Speaker, for the old age pensioners because of our ability to pay more money. I do not plead for them because of pity for them. I do not plead for them for the sake of a market for the farmers. I do not plead for them for the sake of election. I plead for them because, if we represent these people in the House of Commons, it is our duty to bring to the floor of this house the needs of those we profess to represent. I feel that they are entitled to more money and that it is a right that ought to be granted to them.
Then there is one other problem that I feel is not being met. I welcome the proposed amendment to the Municipal Grants Act, but that is meeting the situation only a small part of the way. Some day in Canada we shall again be obliged to sit down around the conference table and rethink Canadian confederation. This is going to be a long process, because the problems are many and varied. However, I feel that this year, 10 years before our hundredth national anniversary, would maybe be a good time to begin facing up to the situation.
Here in Ottawa we have a government that collects over 70 per cent of the tax revenue of Canada, yet the major responsibilities for the business of government in Canada are not in Ottawa at all. In my case they are back in Burnaby and in British Columbia. The individual back home, the taxpayer, just has to stop and think for a moment to realize that he gets most from his hospital board, his school board, his municipal council and his provincial government. They are the organizations that give him most of the things he needs. Yet when he considers who gets his tax money he is obliged to realize that it is time we began thinking about this problem that is threatening Canadian institutions more and more as the years go by.
I propose that we have 10 years of time in which to begin to meet the problem. A mere amendment to the Municipal Grants Act is not solving the problem at all. Certainly it is a little bit of relief for some of our municipalities; but the taxes on real estate, which were once the major source of income, have reached their limit. The taxes on Canadian homes and on Canadian farm land are, I feel, as high as they can safely be set. It is time we declared a moratorium on any increase in taxation on real estate in Canada.
I am not a centralizer. I do not feel that this government should bear all the responsi-

bilities of government in Canada. I believe democracy begins at home, and that you build on from there if you want to build a successful democracy. However, I do not believe that you should rob the home of all the money it has and shoulder the home with all the responsibility. I think that situation must be met. I feel that the Canadian people are rational, reasonable and educated enough so that if there is a will to meet the problem, it can be solved and we can go on to the second century of Canadian progress and Canadian development.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that my time has expired. I should like to repeat once again what I said before. In fact we are all worried about that little piece of land we occupy in this House of Commons, and especially that piece of land across from me occupied by government members. Here is another reference to a piece of land. I have reference to the old age pension. It is a quotation we all know, Mr. Speaker:
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I always pay particular attention to this part of this debate. This year I thought the addresses were of a high order. They showed an amount of careful preparation, and the subjects they introduced were well thought out. The addresses were delivered in a very fine manner.
I wish to speak for a short time tonight on the question of the railway strike. In this connection I wish to present a petition which I have received from the clerk of the town of Smiths Falls. In that town there are 1,700 people involved in this strike. This petition did not come to me in the usual way of petitions; it came in the form of a letter. I could not present it in the usual way by filing it with the Clerk or during routine proceedings, because the letter is addressed directly to me. With your consent, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read this petition into the record because of the fact that it is a letter addressed to me. It reads as follows: Municipal Offices Smiths Falls Ontario.
January 8, 1957
Dr. W. G. Blair, M.P.,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Dr. Blair:
At a meeting of our municipal council duly convened on the evening of January 7, 1957, the following resolution was passed for your attention and action thereon:
"Whereas the welfare of the town of Smiths Falls and district is threatened by the railway strike
The Address-Mr. Blair Be it resolved that the mayor convey to the federal member for Lanark county, Dr. W. G. Blair, M.P., this fact and ask him to inform the government of Canada of the urgent need of having the strike settled."
Yours truly,
F. R. Gilroy,
Town Clerk.
Having presented this petition which came in the form of a letter, there are some things I wish to say concerning this strike because it affects a considerable proportion of the people of the riding which I have the honour to represent. The general consensus, so far as I could judge from the addresses in this house, is that this strike is having a very serious effect on the economy of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and that the sooner it is settled the better. We heard one address yesterday from a maritime member concerning conditions around the port of Saint John. We know the situation with respect to the western wheat farmer. We know the effect on industry in Ontario, and I think opinion is unanimous that this strike must be settled as soon as possible.
I was glad to hear today that there was some sign of settlement of this strike by getting these people together. We hear a great deal about automation, and there are people talking about automation now who never even thought of it two weeks ago. Certainly automation is going to make progress, and any person who would say it is not is simply talking in a foolish manner. Automation will proceed, and automation on the railways will increase in the coming years. I think a good example is to go back to conditions in England in 1850 at the time certain improvements were made in the textile industry with the introduction of new looms, whereby it was possible for one workman to do the work that was formerly done by four or five. At the time automation was introduced into the textile industry it was the main industry in the midlands of Britain. These textiles were shipped all over the world. When the new looms came into use people were thrown out of work. There was a great deal of unemployment. There were riots and difficult times in England. It was not easy for people to understand just what was happening, but there must be progress along those lines. Progress will be made in so far as the railroads are concerned.
I had one thing in mind concerning this strike. I admit candidly that I am not so well versed on labour matters, but I am concerned with the matter of safety. I noted that in the report of the conciliation board there was one sentence that cast some doubt on the question of safety. In considering the
114	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blair question of removing the firemen or engineer's helpers, as they have been called, from the locomotives, there was the suggestion that we would try this thing out and if it did not succeed then we could return to the old system. At least that is the way I interpreted that part of the report, that various changes could be made. I confess, sir, that I have not had experience with labour relations but I have had experience with casualties. I cannot get away from the feeling that there should be a full inquiry into this matter. In so far as the firemen are concerned, they have made a statement that this procedure is not safe. I believe that the firemen are a group of highly responsible people, and if it is not safe there should be a full inquiry into the matter.
If it is ruled by an impartial board that automation has proceeded to the point where the other man is not required on the engine, that is one thing; but if there is the slightest element of danger, then that should be taken into consideration. Any person who has had any experience with railroads knows that wrecks have occurred even under present conditions. It is rather difficult to get away from the matter of human error. Sir, I can call to your mind some accidents that have happened in Canada. I can refer to probably one of the worst accidents that ever happened on a railroad; that is the one that occurred at Almonte a few years ago. It was a dreadful accident; and with all the safety devices on the railroad, with good crews and every care being taken, that accident did happen with the resultant loss of life and horrible injury. I am not fully convinced, therefore, that this matter of safety and the question of human error has been dealt with fully as yet. I feel there should be a further inquiry by a board to make absolutely sure the public is protected.
It is all very well to say you can try this out. It is just like driving an automobile; it is a lot easier to fix the automobile than it is to recover from physical injury. I am glad to see that there has been some move toward an inquiry along that line. As I have stated, I will not be fully convinced until I read a report concerning the matter of safety. I want to be absolutely sure the public of Canada is protected from any form of accident. In my opinion this matter of safety is the crux of the whole thing. Either we do require that extra man on the engine or we do not, and that is the matter which must receive careful consideration from any board appointed to investigate the situation.
Another aspect of the strike with which I am concerned is the matter of people employed in public utilities. I know I am suggesting something very difficult, but it would


seem to me that those employed in public utilities-I am thinking of such public utilities as the hydro, police force and firemen, without whom we cannot get along-should work out some formula or some device for conciliation between the employer, which is generally a municipality or a province, and those working in the public utility. I feel it would be better for such a move to come from labour. It is a very difficult thing to work out, I admit, but if a move were made along that line I think it would be of benefit to all concerned.
I wish to turn for a few minutes to the question of agriculture. I was glad to note the other day in the speech from the throne that some consideration would be given to the question of submarginal land and the possibility of using some device such as the prairie farm rehabilitation act. We go back in the history of this country to the time when the pioneers came here. In going across the country it is very easy to see the areas in which these pioneers settled. They took the high land, and the valleys and lower parts of the country were not utilized at first. They cleared the timber right off the land because it was their ambition to put in crops of some kind to carry them through the ensuing season.
Since that time we have carried on a program of cutting down everything in the nature of timber. I have seen areas in the country where anything that would make a small piece of timber seemed to have been ruthlessly cut down. We have formed no program for the replacement of those trees. This is becoming very important now, because there is usually a spring run-off and there are no trees to hold back the water. The water goes down the streams very rapidly, and we are trying to correct that by building reserve dams.
That is not the answer, Mr. Speaker. We should have a program in this country something like that which has been adopted in some of the Scandinavian countries, namely, if you cut down a tree, plant a tree. There are places in some of the older areas of Canada which do require reforestation, because some of the land was not suitable for farming when it was first cleared. There are other areas which are now classed as submarginal land, which could be used if that land had not been mined but had received proper crop rotation, and if the farmer could have afforded to place fertilizer on the land.
You hear remarks made by economists in agriculture that the time is coming, because of the new type of machinery that is available at the present time, when the larger farm will be the only type of agricultural

unit that will pay. I for one would be very sorry to see some of these smaller farms discontinue operations. The usual description is family farms. I cannot help but think of the fine families that were raised on those farms and the contribution they made to the economy of this country. But I do believe that some of the farms that are worked out at the present time have been mined on account of the fact that farming is becoming a difficult financial venture. I believe that some of those farms could be brought back by the proper use of fertilizer and crop rotation, and that the situation is not hopeless. But there are abandoned farms, Mr. Speaker, the occupants of which have become discouraged. You will find them working in industry. They are not doing any practical farming but are living in the houses on the farms and spending their time in industry. The general complaint of farmers across the country, and especially in my part of the country, is that the prices received for farm products have not kept pace with the prices of consumer goods that the farmer buys. They will all tell you that. This is becoming very apparent to the farmer and is causing many of them to leave the farms; and it is discouraging many young people from entering into the occupation of farming.
Then there is another thing. There has been a steady upward movement in the cost of living. It has gone steadily up in the last three months. I was rather surprised and sorry to note the other day that while the added cost of living was due to various things, there was one thing that seemed to balance out the other way, namely the lower price received for farm products. From the reports we receive I am quite sure that 1957 may be a better year in agricultural circles so far as prices are concerned. There has been the feeling that it may be slightly better than it has been the last four years. Toward the end of last year there was some rise in the prices of agricultural products, and 1957 may be a better year, or equal to 1954; but net farm income will be hundreds of millions of dollars less than the record year of 1951 because costs were lower in 1951 than they were in 1956. Retail prices of food in the stores in 1951 were about the same as they were in 1956, but freight costs, wages and processing costs have increased.
I am going to quote one very well-known authority on agriculture, namely Mr. Bryan L. White, for whose judgment on agricultural matters I have the greatest respect. In the farm page of the Ottawa Journal he points out this fact:
The Address-Mr. Blair There is only one deduction for any fair-minded person to draw from these facts. It is that the farmers of Canada have practically paid for all costs added to food since 1951.
Mr. White was referring to the matter of costs and farm income in the years 1951 to 1956, and he went on to say this:
Wages in the food processing industry have advanced every year, packaging has cost more, but few if any of these costs have been reflected in consumer prices. They have all been deducted at the bottom from the farmer.
I did mention, sir, that I was interested in this committee. I hope when the committee makes its report on the so-called submarginal land it will remember other things, namely that it is necessary to have trees to preserve water; and if industry is going to grow in a province such as Ontario recognition must be given to the enormous amount of water that is used by industry at the present time. Water has become precious. The building of reserve dams will not fully cover the whole matter. It is necessary that we learn and progress more along the line of reforestation, and also consider the deleterious effect of erosion on land.
The matter of reforestation is something that is very important at the present time, but it is difficult to get people to understand it. When our ancestors came to this country it had immense forest cover, but we are only beginning to realize that we cannot proceed without doing something to bring back the land. I remember talking to a forestry man in the Ontario government. I mentioned a part of the country to him and asked why we could not cover those thousands and thousands of acres with pine trees. The land was originally covered with white pine. He made a remark that amazed me. He pointed out that this land had been burned over and it would really take hundreds of years before the land would again become capable of growing pine trees.
It is not a foolish project to carry on a reforestation program, because in time the timber will begin to pay as it did years ago when the land was first cleared, when the trees were sold in the form of squared timber and mighty rafts went down the river to Quebec. The market for squared timber was one of the principal markets of our earlier pioneers.
There is one other matter that I wish to talk about tonight, sir, and that is some of the things that are misunderstood in so far as public relations are concerned between urban and rural dwellers. There is one matter that is really very interesting, because the other night I heard a man speaking on the radio who was evidently a trainer
116	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blair of athletes. He was talking about the harmful effect of milk. There are people talking about this who do not know what they are talking about, because we have always regarded milk as being the perfect food. If this propaganda goes out from people who do not know what they are talking about it will have a harmful effect on the dairy industry.
Medical research has been carried on into the cause of some heart conditions. The work is not yet completed, but there is a feeling that various animal fats have something to do with the causes. When we consider that for years children have been raised on milk-and we believe that milk is a perfect food-it would seem to me that we must attack this problem with common sense, because the eating of fats, or the eating of anything, is all a question of temperance and how you use it. The overeating of any particular type of food is a foolish thing.
This idea is taking hold in the public mind, possibly due to the fact that people read in the paper of the large number of citizens who seem to have developed heart conditions. This is to the detriment of the Canadian dairy industry. This has not yet been advocated by dietitians, and the question of temperance enters into this matter. As I have said, intemperance with regard to any form of food could produce the same effect.
The Prime Minister, in speaking of the matter of health yesterday, made mention of the fact that men in public life and those occupying high positions were subject to great strain and stress, and that the demands of their positions were having a bad effect as far as their physical condition was concerned. The day before yesterday we had the resignation of Hon. George Drew the leader of this party due to ill health, and yesterday brought word of the resignation of Sir Anthony Eden for the same reason. Sir Anthony Eden underwent a most difficult operation three years ago, and those who are his political enemies could very well bear in mind that here is a man who carried on and did a job for his country despite his physical condition. The President of the United States, General Eisenhower, has had difficulties with his health, as has Mr. Dulles. I fully agree with the Prime Minister that the strain and stress of public life is taking its toll among people who are at the head of governments and those who occupy prominent positions. No matter what our political affiliation may be, I feel we should take this into consideration and a measure of sympathy should be extended toward these people.
Before I leave the question of agriculture I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail this morning.


The article is somewhat interesting, and it concerns the health of farmers. It seems that in the southern United States there is an organization known as the international federation of agricultural producers. The Louisiana State University school of medicine conducted a survey in which this organization was interested. The survey revealed that more than 60 per cent of the population of the United States suffers from headaches. The investigation also revealed that medical students had more recurring headaches than anyone else in the country, while farmers had fewer than any other group. This is not a joke; it is a report of the survey made by the Louisiana State University school of medicine. The article goes on to say:
It was not suggested that farmers have less to worry about than other people. The reason for fewer headaches on the farm may be that farmers breathe more fresh air.
I have inserted this in my address because I thought it contained a touch of humour. I am perfectly sure that if farmers do not suffer the physical ills of headaches they certainly suffer headaches in the slang sense of that word. It is a fact that the returns from the sale of farm products have not kept pace with the increased cost of living to the farmer. That is the issue which is causing so much difficulty for the farmer at the present time.
There is one other matter contained in the speech from the throne with which I should like to deal, and that is the question of aid to municipalities. Every person in this chamber, every home owner, and every person who rents in this country is becoming increasingly aware of the fact that taxation on real estate has reached the saturation point; there is no doubt about that. I noticed a statement made by the premier of the province of Ontario a few months ago. He said he had to deal with the reception of 750,000 additional children in primary and elementary schools within the next nine years. This simply means the province of Ontario and its municipalities must make arrangements for the education of almost double the number of pupils they have at the present time.
It is going to be extremely difficult for the municipalities to meet that increased demand by the addition of elementary and high schools. In the same period of time the universities will also double the number of students they have. This is a most serious matter. The young people of this country are our greatest asset. Meeting the increased demands involves in addition to education the supplying of public utilities, sewers, roads, highways, and all the things that are dealt with by the municipalities.

There is no doubt but that real estate has reached its saturation point in terms of taxation, and that at some stage in the next few years we must make arrangements for increased expenditures. I have grave doubts that the broadening of the taxation field through an increase in population or increased industrial expansion will entirely cope with this matter. With regard to aid to the municipalities, any thought the government has given to this matter and any start it makes, no matter how small it may be, will be a step toward some realization of the position of the municipalities. If conditions do not change in the next nine or ten years we are going to be faced with a serious problem. In some way or other there must be a means of granting increased aid to the municipalities.
There are other matters, sir, which I might mention at this time, and one is the position of the veterans. Before I left my home last week I watched a television program which dealt with an institute that cares for homeless men, men in a difficult financial position; as a matter of fact it is a mission. During the program the superintendent of this mission interviewed some of the men who were enjoying a free meal there. In many cases they were returned soldiers, and some reported that they received the veterans allowance. Others said they were not able to work because of their age or state of health, and some were not in receipt of a pension adequate to provide them with a room, meals and the comforts of life.
There is one group of ex-soldiers for whom I wish to make a special appeal. I refer to the soldiers of the first war who served only in England, and who are not eligible for veterans allowance. It is important to remember that they feel they have just as much right to receive the war veterans allowance as do members of the second war who served only in England. This feeling was created possibly because a theatre of war was declared with regard to one war and not with regard to the other. Many of the men who served only in England in the first war were held in position there, and some were ill or unfit. It was through no fault of their own. They made themselves useful in their positions. If you have had any experience in the army you will be aware it is not a good thing to take a man away from a job he is doing well.
Those who served in the first war are growing old, and they are few in number. They look at their comrades who served in the second war, many of whom served only a short time in England, and they feel they are
The Address-Mr. Caron being discriminated against because they are not receiving the war veterans allowance. Certainly their hearts were in the right place when they enlisted, and it is not their fault that they are not eligible. They are becoming older and fewer in number all the time.
In view of the decreasing number of these old gentlemen, who with the best possible motives enlisted in the first world war, I ask the government to reconsider the matter of war veterans allowances and grant allowances to those who served in England in the first world war. As I watched the movie showing these men being fed I felt that there was something wrong when they were forced to obtain a meal at a mission in order to keep body and soul together. Certainly this parliament should do something.
There are not many of them, and it would not cost this country very much. I hope no member of the government will say that we of the opposition ask the government to spend money and at the same time ask the government to save money. This is a small matter, and it does not enter into the question of spending money. It is the duty of Canada to look after these aged citizens who with the best motives volunteered in the first world war.
I know some of these men personally. They have no pensions, as they are in between the age groups. The average age of men who served in the first world war is in the early sixties, and many of them are not eligible for the old age pension with a means test. They are receiving nothing. The fact that they served should be recognized. I know it would be the wish of every Canadian that these people not be neglected.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks, I wish to join with the hon. members who have already congratulated the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Hanna and Mr. Robichaud), who carried out their particular function in a splendid and masterful fashion. They spoke as statesmen, and we thank them for enlightening the house on many subjects.
Since the last session, important changes have taken place in this house, especially on the other side where we see a new leader of the opposition. I wonder if I must congratulate him or commiserate with him. A mixture of both feelings is appropriate, I guess. I must congratulate him for the support he received from his friends of the Conservative party who gave him a majority on the very first ballot. On the other hand, it seems that I must commiserate with him as he has entered a field fraught with difficulties. He

The Address-Mr. Caron will have to bear a very heavy burden, and I hope that Divine Providence will give him the strength and courage to do so, for, even if he should come back to this house as leader of the opposition after the election, I must say to him that it is no dishonour to remain in that post for a long time.
We have been speaking quite extensively in this house about the well known question of Suez, and some people have gone as far as to suggest that the behaviour of the Canadian government during the crisis had endangered the future of the British commonwealth. I wonder if those people have bothered to study the matter with sufficient thoroughness.
When Israel invaded Egypt, for reasons which they explained clearly enough from their own point of view, France and England immediately undertook their own invasion, thus leaving peace in a most delicate position.
The Canadian government's position with regard to this matter has, to my mind, been most commendable. The representative of the Canadian government to the United Nations, the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), did not want to condemn either England or France, but he nevertheless tried to maintain peace in the world with a reasonable suggestion. He therefore asked, by means of a resolution, that France and England withdraw their troops from Egypt and that the United Nations replace them with a force that would be responsible for maintaining peace and preventing invaders of any country from returning to this area.
The position of the Canadian government under those circumstances has been commended by almost all the countries of the globe. The United States took this opportunity to support the proposal made by our government because they also sought universal peace. That is why I hold that, by its action, the Canadian government did not endanger the British commonwealth. On the contrary, by its attitude, it merely consolidated its relations, because the commonwealth was on the verge of losing the support of India and of some other countries of the East who wanted to leave the commonwealth as a result of England's attitude. Since then, our union has been once more strengthened. Recently we received in this country the visit of the prime minister of India who came to hold talks with our own Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) about affairs of concern to the whole world. He believes that the whole world needs Canada's help. He knows that our country has been capable of stopping to reflect on matters, of taking no account of its own particular preferences, of looking facts in the face and of attempting to protect that peace for which we have so often fought in the past.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that Canada now deserves to be considered as one of the most enlightened countries in the whole world and that our leaders have acted in a most admirable fashion.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the time, I propose the adjournment of the debate.

On motion of Mr. Caron the debate was adjourned.
